bio.en: Elena Verna is the Head of Growth at Lovable, the AI vibe-coding platform that surpassed $200 million in ARR within roughly a year of launch with a team of about 100 people.
bio.zh: Elena Verna 是 Lovable 的增长负责人，Lovable 是一个 AI vibe coding 平台，在发布约一年内、以约 100 人的团队实现了超过 2 亿美元的年度经常性收入（ARR）。

summary.en: Elena explains that in the AI era, product-market fit is no longer a one-time milestone but a recurring fight you must recapture every three months as both the underlying technology and consumer expectations shift rapidly. She shares Lovable's growth playbook: giving the product away for free and treating LLM costs as marketing spend, building a lively community on Discord, building in public, and embedding activation inside the product/AI team rather than a separate growth team. On hiring and culture, she argues AI-native new grads and failed founders are now the hottest talent, and that women risk being left behind in the AI wave unless we deliberately create on-ramps like Lovable's SheBuilds hackathons. She also reflects on work-life balance at a hyper-growth startup and why ruthlessly protecting personal boundaries is essential to doing your best work.
summary.zh: Elena 指出，在 AI 时代，产品市场契合不再是一次性的里程碑，而是一场每三个月就得重新抓住的持久战——因为底层技术和消费者期望都在快速变化。她分享了 Lovable 的增长打法：把产品免费送出去、把 LLM 成本当作营销开支，在 Discord 上建设活跃的社区，公开构建，以及把"激活"嵌入产品/AI 团队而不是单独的增长团队。在招聘和文化上，她认为 AI 原生的新毕业生和失败过的创始人现在是抢手人才，而女性若不加以刻意铺路（如 Lovable 的 SheBuilds 黑客松）很容易在这波 AI 浪潮中被落下。她还聊了超高速增长创业公司的工作生活平衡，以及为什么 ruthlessly 地保护个人边界，是把工作做到最好的前提。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're ahead of growth at Lovable on track to be the fastest or one of the fastest growing companies in history.
turns.zh: 你在 Lovable 管增长，正走在成为史上最快、或最快之一增长公司的路上。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: We're over 200 million in ARR. At this point, we're 100 people large, the pace here is insane.
turns.zh: 我们 ARR 已经过 2 亿美元。到现在，我们大概 100 人，这节奏太疯狂了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You said that you've had to throw out most of your growth playbook.
turns.zh: 你说你不得不把大部分增长手册扔掉。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: I feel like only 30 to 40% of what I've learned in the last 15 to 20 years of being in growth transfers here because we just need to invest in such bigger bets, and innovate, and create new growth loops here, everybody and their mother is starting a vibe coding business nowadays, and we need to figure out how to be ahead of them. And to be ahead of them is not optimization of the problem, it's reinvention of the solution. I just feel like I usually spend maybe 5% innovating on growth in my previous roles, right now, I'm spending 95% innovating on growth, and only 5% on optimization.
turns.zh: 我觉得我过去 15 到 20 年学到的增长经验，只有 30% 到 40% 能搬到这里。因为我们得投更大的赌注、去创新、在这里造出新的增长循环。现在人人和他妈都在开 vibe coding（氛围编程）生意，我们得想怎么走在他们前头。而走在前面靠的不是优化问题，而是重塑解法。我一般在我以前的角色里大概只花 5% 在增长创新上，现在我在增长创新上花 95%，优化只花 5%。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you find is actually moving the needle?
turns.zh: 那你觉得什么真正在起作用？

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: One of our biggest strategy is building in public, and it's coupled with employee socials, founder-led socials. And another one is giving your product away a lot, this is part of our growth secret sauce. You have to remove the barrier of entry. If somebody, one of our users stands up and say, hey, I'm going to have a hackathon at my work on Lovable, can you give us some free credits to play with? Why would we prevent a person who wants to do all of the marketing and activating for us from using us? We're like, take it, how much do you need?
turns.zh: 我们最大的策略之一是"公开构建"（building in public），再配上员工社媒、创始人主导的社媒。另一个是把产品大量送出去，这也是我们的增长秘方之一。你得移除进入门槛。如果我们某个用户站起来说"嘿，我要在我公司办个 Lovable 黑客松，能给点免费额度玩玩吗？"——我们凭什么去拦一个愿意替我们做营销、做激活的人用我们？我们就会说，拿去，你要多少？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The trick is get more people to try it, just ship things you can talk about.
turns.zh: 诀窍就是让更多人去试，去发布那些你能拿来讲的东西。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: The only way to create a word of mouth loop is just to blow their socks off.
turns.zh: 要造出口碑循环，唯一的办法就是把他们的袜子都惊掉。

turns.en: Thank you for having me.
turns.zh: 谢谢你邀我。

turns.zh: 我爱这个。谢谢你又邀我，在这一点上我这个纪录保持者挺自豪的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I love about you coming back each time, it feels like every time you come back, you're just doing something even more epic and exciting. And so, these days, as we'll hear in the intro, you're head of growth at Lovable, which no big deal on track to be the fastest or one of the fastest growing companies in history, depending on the metric that you track. Let's talk about just the scale and growth of Lovable to give people a sense of just how incredible this is. I'll share a bit of this in intro, but just what are some stats you can share about just how things are going Lovable?
turns.zh: 我喜欢你每次回来，感觉都更史诗、更带劲。所以如今，就像你会在 intro 听到的，你是 Lovable 的增长负责人——没什么大不了的，正走在成为史上最快或最快之一增长公司的路上，看你怎么衡量。我们先聊聊 Lovable 的规模和增长，让人感受下这有多不可思议。intro 里我分享了一些，但你能分享些数据，说明 Lovable 现在到底怎么样？

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: So, we are just a little bit over one year's old since we launched. The company actually did exist as a GPT engineer before, but it officially launched in the third week of November last year, in 2024. So, for us, we've hit over $200 million in annual recurring revenue before we even hit our one-year milestone since being launched. Which is pretty incredible. You, Lenny, actually have a really great blog post on how quickly it takes for companies usually to get to their first million ARR, and it's usually multiple years. So, this is definitely a unicorn, I don't think this is a standard. There's a couple of things that account for it, and we can talk about it, and the growth is only accelerating, so it's compounding, which is great. Because we had our 100 million in end of July, and just four months later we were at 200 million. (00:07:02): So, seven months to, well, maybe eight months, to 100 million, another four months to get to 200 million. And from users too, we already have over eight million users that have tried Lovable, we have, as you can imagine, to feed that 200 million, hundreds of thousands of paid subscribers as well that are paying for us, so things are going great and we'll talk about why.
turns.zh: 我们正式上线才刚过一年。这公司以前其实叫 GPT Engineer 存在过，但正式上线是去年 2024 年 11 月的第三周。所以对我们来说，上线还不到一年里程碑，ARR 就过了 2 亿美元。挺不可思议的。Lenny 你其实有篇很棒的博客，讲公司通常要多久才到第一个百万 ARR，一般是好几年。所以这是个独角兽，我不觉得这是常态。有几件事促成它，我们可以聊，而且增长还在加速、在复利，这很好。因为我们 7 月底到 1 亿，仅仅四个月后就到 2 亿了。所以七个月、好吧也许八个月到 1 亿，再四个月到 2 亿。用户上，我们已经有超过 800 万试过 Lovable 的用户，可想而知，要喂出那 2 亿，也有几十万付费订阅用户在给我们付钱，所以一切都很棒，我们聊聊为什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Absurd. I think people are getting used to these insane numbers, and not long ago is like, okay, if you hit a million ARR in a year, you're doing pretty well.
turns.zh: 离谱。我觉得人们正在习惯这些疯数字，不久之前还是"哦你一年做到 100 万 ARR，你干得不错"。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. I think still you're doing pretty well if you have a million ARR in one year. This is one of the once in a lifetime type of companies, and the category, the way that it's evolving. So, I want to make sure that people don't all of a sudden set this as a benchmark for success because it should never be. In some categories, it might be even faster as we continue evolving technology, but I don't think that it's realistic to expect it out of your business that you're starting right now.
turns.zh: 对，对。我觉得如果你一年有 100 万 ARR，还是干得不错的。这是那种一辈子遇一次的公司的类型，还有这个品类演进的方式。所以我想确保大家别突然把这当成成功基准，因为它绝不该是。某些品类，随着技术继续演进，可能甚至更快，但我不觉得你正起步的生意能现实地期待这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such an important point you're making there, it's so discouraging to founders to hear these stories of getting 200 million. And again, this is ARR. There's a lot of companies, especially in the data labeling space, I've had them all on the podcast, that are very fast-growing, but they're not recurring revenue. There's also, they pay out their people to do this data labeling. So, the revenue numbers there don't really equate. Recurring $200 million a year is absurd.
turns.zh: 你这点太重要了，听这种 2 亿的故事对创始人很打击信心。再说，这是 ARR。很多公司，尤其在数据标注领域，我都请上过播客，增长很快，但不是经常性收入。而且他们还要付钱让人做标注。所以那边的营收数字其实不对等。经常性的一年 2 亿，太离谱了。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yeah, it is absurd. I really want to make sure that people understand as we go through this episode as to why it's happening, because part of it is on Lovable, part of it is just in the market and how it's moving. So, when you're setting yourself as a benchmark, so you know which benchmarks you actually to use, and whether Lovable is the benchmark that you should be using.
turns.zh: 对，是离谱。我特别想让大家在听这期时明白它为什么发生，一部分在 Lovable，一部分就在市场、在它怎么动。所以当你拿它当基准时，你得知道该用哪些基准、Lovable 到底是不是你该用的基准。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. I'm going to get into that next. Last question, just I want to see what you can share here. A lot of people look at these numbers, a lot of people are very skeptical these are lasting, durable numbers. Like who are these people? How is there $200 million being spent on Lovable? Anything you can add about, just give people confidence, is this real, this is going to last, this is a really durable business.
turns.zh: 酷。下一段我就聊这个。最后一个问题，就想看你能分享什么。很多人看这些数字，很多人很怀疑这些是不是持久、扎实的数字。这些人是谁？那 2 亿是怎么花在 Lovable 上的？你能补点什么，给人信心——这是真的、会持久、这是个很扎实的生意？

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Well, I saw Stripe receipts, so it is real, as far as I'm concerned, unless Stripe dashboard is lying to us. But it is money getting deposited in our bank account. But let's talk about who is actually contributing to that number. We do have a really large use case of people starting their own companies on Lovable, so we call it a founder use case. Where somebody that is non-technical, that has never been able to code or create a piece of software is now able to come in and actually build an app completely from scratch. And some of them are already monetizing it, some of it just using it [inaudible 00:09:52] for other services, or some physical goods, for example, that they're selling. Some of them are just still building. And we monetize on the act of building, so that progression of building up to your product market fit takes quite a bit of time. (00:10:06): And even with Lovable, we're so much more efficient and effective compared to hiring an engineer in terms of the price, but it still takes time. So, we have a lot of founders, whether it's B2C, whether there's B2B, so consumer products, business products, e-commerce, whatever it is. But on the other side, we have a lot of employees within companies using Lovable as well, where they're building internal tools, or they're building prototypes, they're building landing pages. So, that is another use case that is very relevant and quite efficient for us, but then there is a hype and discovery that is happening as well. Because when I think about software, I think about it, I talked to John Cutler actually, and he gave me this framework that is completely stuck in my mind, of software always goes through capabilities stage first, so what is possible to actually create with this? (00:11:00): Then, it needs to transition into value, of how is it that am I going to get value out of this? And then you can start thinking about scaling it, of which aspects of my life and my work that can actually go in? And we're right now very much in the capability stage with vibe coding, because everybody's just exploring, what can I do? And the beautiful thing here is that what you can do changes every month to three months. So, you constantly need to come back and you need to see what has changed. So, a lot of people use it for personal reasons. I build myself apps, tutoring apps for my kid, so he has to answer questions in order to get some screen time accumulated for him. I build my own portfolio. (00:11:40): I see people doing wonderful things, my favorite story that I always say, there's this man that created a proposal on Lovable. So, his fiance had to answer questions and she had to complete this game, and then at the end there was this big reveal and he proposed to her. But people just unlock the most creative things that they build on Lovable, and that's where the revenue is coming from. The one piece that is working very well for us in terms of how our monetization model is, set up and how it interjects with your activation moment, which we can also cover, but that is what's driving both conversion and retention rates.
turns.zh: 嗯，我看过 Stripe 回单，所以就我所知是真的，除非 Stripe 后台在骗我们。但钱确实是打进我们银行账户的。但我们聊聊到底是谁在贡献这个数字。我们有一个很大的使用场景：人们在 Lovable 上开自己的公司，我们叫"创始人使用场景"。就是那种非技术背景、从没码过代码或做过软件的人，现在能进来、从零完整搭个 app。有些人已经在变现了，有些拿它[听不清]做别的服务，或卖实体货。有些还在建。而我们是按"构建"这个动作变现的，所以从构建走到产品市场匹配要挺长时间。即便用 Lovable，比起雇工程师，我们在价格和效率上都高太多，但还是得花时间。所以我们有很多创始人，B2C 也好、B2B 也好，消费产品、商业产品、电商，什么都有。但另一头，我们也有很多企业里的员工在用 Lovable 建内部工具、做原型、做落地页。所以这是另一个很相关、对我们也很高效的使用场景。但除此之外还有 hype 和发现在发生。因为说到软件，我和 John Cutler 聊过，他给了我一个框架，彻底粘在我脑子里：软件总是先经过"能力阶段"——用这东西到底能造出什么？然后它需要过渡到"价值"——我怎么从它身上拿到价值？再然后你才开始想规模化，我生活和工作的哪些方面能真正放进去？而我们在 vibe coding 上，现在非常处在能力阶段，因为大家都在探索：我能做什么？而美妙的是，你能做的事每过一到三个月就变。所以很多人为了个人原因用。我自己就建 app，给我孩子做个辅导 app，他得答题才能攒到屏幕时间。我建自己的作品集。我看到人们做奇妙的事，我最爱说的故事是：有个男的在 Lovable 上做了个求婚。他未婚妻得答题、得玩完这个游戏，最后有个大揭晓，他向她求婚了。但人们就解锁了最富创意的东西，在 Lovable 上建出来，那正是营收来源。对我们特别奏效的一点，是我们的变现模型怎么设、以及它怎么插进你的激活时刻——这个我们也能聊——但那是同时驱动转化率和留存率的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me ask you one question that's on people's minds, I imagine, as you talk about this, just what does retention look like?
turns.zh: 让我问你一个很多人心里估计都在想的问题——说到这，留存长什么样？

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yeah. So, retention, really, I look at it in two ways, retention, that it comes as a subscriber retention. So, how much [inaudible 00:12:32] subscribers do we get, and how many of them are we capable of renewing? There's also very important aspect of it is, how many of them can we expand? Because if you can get positive or above 100% net dollar retention, which is super important metric for investors... If you don't know about net dollar retention, please read it up, that's like a superpower to get bigger multiple if you can show NDR that is over 100. And then there's actually engagement retention as well, because that is the leading indicator for how your paid retention is going to look like. For paid retention, I know there is so much on the market of, oh, this is a high product, and it's a leaky bucket, and it has really high churn rates. (00:13:10): Although, I shouldn't share, it's not public numbers for us to share actual retention, however, what I can say, it's on par with benchmarks of other B2B SaaS products that I've ever worked at. And I worked with Miro, Dropbox, SurveyMonkey, Netlify, Amplitude, and others. So, are we absolutely crushing with paid retention? No. Are we where most of the other companies are? Yes. Our NDR is quite good because when people build, they want to buy more credits to build. So, we're seeing really good revenue retention, but we're honestly more focused right now on engagement retention than even paid retention because our North Star is just to get as much usage as possible, and we will fix and tune our monetization model afterwards. So, engagement retention, I would say, is a by far bigger priority focus for us at the moment.
turns.zh: 对。所以留存，我其实从两个角度看：一种是订阅留存，我们有多少订阅者、又能续回多少？另一块很重要：我们能扩展多少？因为如果你能做到正的、或 100% 以上的净收入留存（NDR），对投资人是个超级重要的指标……如果你不知道净收入留存，去读一下，能展示超过 100 的 NDR 是拿到更高估值的超能力。还有参与留存，因为它是你付费留存的先行指标。说到付费留存，市场上有很多"哦这是高产品、是个漏桶、流失率超高"的说法。虽然我不该透露，实际留存数字不是公开的，但我能说：它和我待过的其他 B2B SaaS 产品的基准持平。我待过 Miro、Dropbox、SurveyMonkey、Netlify、Amplitude 等。所以我们把付费留存碾压了吗？没有。我们和其他公司一样吗？是的。我们的 NDR 相当好，因为人们建东西时，想买更多额度来建。所以营收留存很好，但现在我们对参与留存的重视远超付费留存，因为我们的北极星就是尽量拉高使用量，变现模型之后再去调。所以参与留存，目前绝对是我们的头号重心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is incredibly interesting, and I'm optimistic to hear because of the growth rate. Rarely is growth rate this high and retention is on par with great companies.
turns.zh: 这太有意思了，而且听你这么说我很乐观，因为增长这么高。很少见到增长率这么高、同时留存还能和优秀公司持平的。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yeah. And I'll just say too, which is a little bit maybe counterintuitive would be to a lot of companies, we don't optimize for revenue at all. In fact, internally, we have a lot of discussions about how can we give more products away, how can we reduce our revenue growth rate by just getting more paid subscribers, more users using Lovable, to just get bigger share of the market. So, our revenue is an outcome of us just trying to get more people through the door, not us trying to optimize for revenue per user, or to get them to monetize at the higher rate. So, there's a very interesting path here, where, by actually focusing on the inputs, like you should, it translates to a good output, but we don't look at that output as something that we're trying to grow.
turns.zh: 对。我还想说一点，对很多公司可能有点反直觉：我们根本不优化营收。事实上，内部我们大量讨论的是怎么把更多产品送出去、怎么靠拉更多付费订阅者、更多用户来用 Lovable、去拿更大的市场份额，从而降低我们的营收增速。所以我们的营收，只是我们想让更多人进门的结果，而不是我们去优化每用户营收、或让他们以更高档变现的结果。所以这里有条很有意思的路径：像你该做的那样，真正聚焦在投入上，它自然转化成好的产出，但我们不把那个产出当成我们要去增长的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's talk about growth, let's talk about what you've learned about growth in this space. You had this post online where you said that you've had to throw out most of your growth playbook. This is a huge deal, you've led growth a lot of really successful companies. Lovable is growing incredibly well, this tells me there's a lot we can learn from what you've seen. So, tell us what you're seeing, what's still working, what's not working, what you've learned about what it takes to drive growth at a company like Lovable.
turns.zh: 我们聊聊增长，聊聊你在这个领域学到的增长。你在网上有篇帖子说，你不得不把大部分增长手册扔掉。这是大事，你带过很多超成功公司的增长。Lovable 长得这么好，这告诉我，从你看到的里面我们能学到很多。所以，告诉我们你在看什么、什么还在管用、什么不管用了、你学到了什么——在一家像 Lovable 这样的公司，驱动增长需要什么。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yeah. I would say that in any other role that I've come into before, I felt confident in about 80% of the patterns that I can bring to that role, meaning that I can identify inputs, understand which framework applies. I know a lot of examples that fit in within that framework, so we just need to localize a solution and push, and it was quite productive in terms of getting a company those additional acquisition, conversion, engagement, monetization rates. So, I felt very repetitive in a way, after some time, because I feel like I'm just coming in and copy, pasting, copy, pasting... And although every single company loves to say that they have unique problems, at the end of the day, all of the problems were very similar. And I felt like I was doing the same job over and over again. When I started at Lovable, the one thing to me that was very clear is that this company was growing like crazy before I joined. (00:16:21): So, I want to make sure that there's not that much value on what I have even added today, because this company is on the tear, and yes, we're rounding the edges and removing barriers for growth, so we're not standing in our own way, but there's something more magical happening here that is not a pattern that I've ever seen before. It's not a framework that I can even conceptualize in my head. And plus, it's a new category that I've never seen, or I've never been in a company that is in a new emerging category, that hits fast moving water so quickly. And that's the difference because when you're usually trying to create a new category, it takes years. I know it's every marketer's dream to create a new category, but it takes decades often to really get that much hype and adoption around it. Versus with vibe coating, this hype seemed to have happened really quickly. (00:17:16): It's like it's hit the nerve with the market. So, yes, we're at the right place, we're at the right time, but we're also in really fast moving waters, and the demand that is coming to us, we need to capture it mostly, we don't need to generate a lot of it yet. But at the same time, it comes with the really big downfalls of we're not in control of a lot of our growth. Let's be honest about it, there's so much incredible word of mouth that is happening, and we're trying to grow that, but to enable as much of that as possible, but the company is moving, we're just hanging on to it as fast as possible, and making sure that we're not going to hit a wall, so to speak, in front of us, and that the wheels are greased, and that all of the pieces are in places. It's like your race car framework that you have as well. (00:18:05): We're really just putting a lot of oil into it, and figuring out what is our engine actually going to be that is going to take us forward. But when I'm thinking about the patterns here, and what I have to unlearn, I feel like only 30 to 40% of what I've learned in the last 15 to 20 years of being in growth transfers here. And some of it is very straightforward, okay, this is how you're going to do paid marketing, this is how you're going to do some of the habitual retention, here's the free to pay maybe monetization frameworks that still stand. But the rest of it, honestly, it doesn't feel like it even matters anymore, because we just need to invest in such bigger bets, and innovate, and create new growth loops here, as opposed to trying to optimize it to the moon and beyond, which I usually be focused on in a scaled business like this.
turns.zh: 对。我会说，在我以前进过的任何角色，我对能带过去的模式大概有 80% 的信心——也就是我能识别输入、知道哪个框架适用、我有很多符合那框架的例子，所以只要把方案本地化、推下去，就能很高效地给公司带来额外的获客、转化、参与、变现。所以一段时间后会觉得自己在重复，因为我好像就是进去、复制粘贴、复制粘贴……虽然每家公司都爱说自己的问题独特，但说到底所有问题都很像。我觉得自己在一遍遍做同一份工作。当我加入 Lovable 时，一件很清楚的事是：这公司在我来之前就已经疯长。所以我想确保别高估我到现在加了多少价值，因为这公司在狂奔，没错，我们在打磨边缘、移除增长的绊脚石，好不挡自己路，但这里有更魔性的事在发生，那是我从没见过的模式、是我脑子里都概念化不出来的框架。再加上，这是个我从没见过的新品类，我从没待过这么快冲进急流的新兴品类公司。这就是区别——因为通常你创一个新品类要花好几年。我知道每个市场人都梦想创品类，但往往要几十年才能真正有那种 hype 和采用。而 vibe coding 的 hype 似乎发生得极快。它像是戳中了市场的神经。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's follow those threads. So, what is it that no longer is worth it in this bucket of just like, let's not spend any time on this thing, and then what do you find is actually moving the needle?
turns.zh: 我们顺着这些线头聊。那在这个"别花时间"的桶里，什么不再值得了？而你又发现什么真正在起作用？

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Not worth it, in growth, most of the people spend most of the time optimizing existing user journeys. So, you already have maybe some of your growth loops that you understand that you try to optimize or you just know, hey, there's big drop-offs from acquisition to activation, let me go figure out how to... I can tweak the dials to get it done. Here, what I find is that optimizations are just not worth our time. So, a lot of the times my growth team actually ends up working on new features, or just standing up new growth loops one after another, and yes, there's of course the saying of more growth loops does not mean more growth, but at the same time, the market is moving so quickly, you need to stand up a bunch of initiatives to capture it because it's perishable. (00:19:54): Or we also have so much competition. We're not alone here, so we can't ignore that there's everybody in their mother is starting a vibe coding business nowadays, and we need to figure out how to be ahead of them. And to be ahead of them is not optimization of the problem, it's reinvention of the solution. So, I just feel like I usually spend maybe 5%, maybe 10% if I'm lucky, innovating on growth in my roles, in my previous roles, right now, I'm spending 95% innovating on growth, and only 5% on optimization. And most of my frameworks are on optimization because it's really hard to come up with frameworks for innovation because by default there, by definition, they're innovative.
turns.zh: 不值得的，是增长里大多数人把大多数时间花在优化现有用户旅程上。你也许已经有些理解的增长循环，你试着优化，或者你就知道"获客到激活掉得厉害，我去想想怎么调旋钮搞定"。在这里，我发现优化根本不值我们的时间。所以我的增长团队很多时候其实在搞新功能，或者一个接一个地立起新的增长循环——当然有那句老话"更多增长循环不等于更多增长"，但同时，市场动得太快，你得立起一堆举措去接住它，因为它是会过期的。或者我们竞争也超多。这里不是我们一家，我们不能忽略"现在人人和他妈都在开 vibe coding 生意"，我们得想怎么走在前头。而走在前头靠的不是优化问题，是重塑解法。所以我一般在我以前角色里大概花 5%，运气好 10%，在增长创新上，现在我花 95% 在增长创新、只 5% 在优化。而我的大多数框架都是关于优化的，因为给创新搞框架太难——按定义，它们就是创新的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I'm hearing here is new features. Launching new features, [inaudible 00:20:42] product is one of the bigger growth levers, versus you have a bunch of cool stuff, make it easier to use, increase activation, reduce friction, things like that.
turns.zh: 我听到的是新功能。发布新功能、[听不清]产品本身就是更大的增长杠杆之一，而不是你有一堆很酷的东西、让它更好用、提升激活、减少摩擦之类的。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yeah. And for example, we on growth team launched integration with Shopify, to enable e-commerce use case, because we're like, hey, there's already people trying to come in and do it, Shopify was open for integration with us, let's go lean into it so people can vibe code their storefronts. That came out of growth, that usually would never come out of growth. Why would growth team ever invest into a core product integration? Or we enabled voice mode for people so they can actually chat with Lovable using their voice, as opposed to only having type. And that's also, it's a feature, it's a core product feature, but we're like, hey, it's going to help people to converse with Lovable more, it's going to increase the engagement. (00:21:32): One area that we've spent very little time in is activation, because usually I spend majority of my time in activation because there's so many awareness things that need to happen, and so many things that we need to smooth out experience for the users in order for them to get through that setup moment, to aha moment, to the habit loop, and here you're just interacting with agent. So, we, at the beginning, we're like, the agent team that we have here is working a lot on it. Why would we go in there and do anything? It's like our core team is responsible for activation. Now, we're starting to move into doing agent work ourselves, so all of a sudden growth team is not just doing product surfaces, now we're doing agentic workflows and codifying agent instructions in order for customers to activate better. (00:22:21): So, the work fundamentally, I feel like has gotten deeper into product, and deeper into actual core product functionality, as opposed to just being a smoothing surface on the outer layers.
turns.zh: 对。比如我们增长团队上线了和 Shopify 的集成，去支撑电商使用场景，因为我们想"嘿，已经有人在试进来了、Shopify 对我们开放集成，那我们就靠上去，让人能 vibe code 他们的店面"。这出自增长团队，通常永远不会出自增长。增长团队凭什么投核心产品集成？或者我们给人开了语音模式，让他们能用声音和 Lovable 聊，而不只是打字。那也是个功能、核心产品功能，但我们想"嘿，这能让人更多和 Lovable 对话，能提升参与"。我们花极少时间在激活上，因为通常我大部分时间都花在激活上——因为有太多认知要把事情办成，有太多东西要给用户顺滑体验、好让他们走过 setup 时刻、到 aha 时刻、到习惯循环，而这里你只是在和 agent 互动。所以一开始我们想"我们的 agent 团队在那儿已经花很多功夫了，我们干嘛进去插手？"那是核心团队的激活职责。现在我们也开始自己动手做 agent 工作，所以增长团队突然不只在做产品表面，现在我们在做 agentic 工作流、把 agent 指令编码固化，好让客户更好激活。所以工作从根本上变得更深进产品、更深进真正的核心产品功能，而不只是外层的一层打磨面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, that is also a very big deal, every growth person that's ever been on this podcast, including you, always talks about the power of activation, just how much opportunity there is to get people to this aha moment, realize the value of this product, that increases retention and increases everything. And what you're saying here is you barely spend any time on activation because in a company like Lovable, there's a prompt, you give it what you want, it generates a thing, and that's basically all it is. And so, the impact is to make that agent better...
turns.zh: 好，这也很重大。每个上过这播客的增长人，包括你，都总在谈激活的威力——让人到 aha 时刻、意识到产品价值，那能提升留存、提升一切。而你说你几乎不花时间在激活上，因为在 Lovable 这种公司，就一个 prompt，你给想要的东西，它生成个东西，基本就是这样。所以影响在于让那个 agent 在那件事上更好……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... basically all it is. And so the impact is to make that agent better at that thing, versus micro-optimize every step.
turns.zh: ……基本就是这样。所以影响在于让那个 agent 在那件事上更好，而不是微优化每一步。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: And our agent team spends night and day thinking about it. So I've never been at a company where core team thinks so much about activation, thinks so much about that first generation, thinks so much about reaching a-ha moment. So it's more weaved in into DNA of the overall company, which takes the pressure off of me to only have to focus on it. Because otherwise, yeah, I would be in that experience all the time. (00:23:32): But I feel a lot more at ease, because everybody's thinking about it and everybody's working on making agents better. And agent, the beauty of it is it doesn't matter if it's actually first generation or if it's your Nth generation. It just needs to be a better generation. Agent needs to understand your intent better, and think and reason behind it. So it improves the entire lifecycle immediately as opposed to having to only work on that first experience per se.
turns.zh: 而且我们的 agent 团队日夜在想这个。我从没待过一家公司，核心团队这么想激活、这么想第一次生成、这么想到达 aha 时刻。所以它更编织进全公司的 DNA，这把"只有我得盯它"的压力卸掉了。否则，对，我会一直泡在那个体验里。但我自在多了，因为大家都在想、都在让 agent 更好。而 agent 的美妙在于，不管它是第一次生成还是第 N 次，它只需要是"更好的一次生成"。Agent 需要更好地理解你的意图、在背后思考和推理。所以它立即改善整个生命周期，而不是只能死磕第一次体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And what you're not saying is, "Don't care about that experience," it's, "The team building that is already obsessed with making that activation experience better and better."
turns.zh: 你没说的是"别管那个体验"，而是"造它的团队已经痴迷于让那个激活体验越来越好"。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Exactly, exactly. I love that, because that's the core product functionality at this point. And before people would spend more time building deeper features, or deeper use cases, or trying to improve some platform functionality. And now the core team, they're obsessed about that first experience because that is core product.
turns.zh: 正是，正是。我爱这个说法，因为那此刻就是核心产品功能。以前人们花更多时间建更深的功能、更深的用例、或试图改进某个平台功能。而现在核心团队痴迷于第一次体验，因为那是核心产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another lever that I've noticed, especially with Lovable, and I'm seeing it more and more on social media is just founders telling you what's going on. I think this connects really deeply with the new features. Launch new features. Say Anton is just like, "Hey, check out this cool new thing. Check out our growth numbers." Is that a big growth lever too?
turns.zh: 我注意到的另一个杠杆，尤其 Lovable，我在社媒上越来越常见，就是创始人亲自跟你讲在干嘛。我觉得这和"新功能"深深相连。发新功能。就像 Anton 直接说"嘿，看这个超酷的新东西。看我们的增长数字。"这也是个大增长杠杆吗？

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yeah. So one of our biggest strategy is building in public. Building in public, and it's coupled with employee socials, founder-led socials for sure. This is difficult for larger companies. But when you're smaller and you still have a little bit more narrative control with everybody on your team, plus you have so much more trust within the organization, where people are going to say the right things because they understand what actually has happened, that ability to just really quickly deliver the message to the market becomes really important. (00:25:21): Now, we still do the big launches, so we still have everything tiered into tier three, two, one. Tier ones are going to happen as big moments that we're going to really rally as a company behind. And it's going to be something that is meant to step function, change our product market fit, and we're going to do a bunch of activities behind it. (00:25:40): But at the same time, what's really important to us is to maintain noise in the market. And that noise in the market happens by us shipping every day, every other day, multiple times per day and just talking about it constantly. Interestingly enough, it's actually works fantastic resurrection strategy, because people are like, "Oh, there's more things here. I need to go check it out." (00:26:03): It also works as a great reengagement strategy. So instead of sending newsletters to say, "Here's the market trends or here's the user stories," people are literally logging into their social to say, "Okay, what has Lovable shipped now?" It's like, "What is the change?" So it's interesting to them to see, because from the time that they voice their opinion on what needs to happen to actual delivery is so short, so they feel heard. And they are heard, because that's how we prioritize all of the things that we're shipping. But it's interesting, because I've never been in a company that tries to maintain so much just shipping velocity to maintain a certain amount of noise that it feels like the product is alive. It's changing every single week. And then there's these big amplifications, turbo boost so to speak, in the race car model, that then go out and they fundamentally create a step function change in that product market fit as a whole. And that is a retention strategy I can get behind any day and all day. I only hope that we can maintain it as we continue scaling.
turns.zh: 对。我们最大的策略之一是"公开构建"。公开构建，再配上员工社媒、创始人主导社媒，肯定。这对大公司很难。但当你更小、对团队每个人的叙事还有更多掌控，加上组织内信任多得多——人们会说出正确的话，因为他们理解实际发生了什么——那种能极快把信息递到市场的能力就变得极重要。我们现在还做大的发布，所以还是有分层的 tier 三、二、一。tier 一是那种大时刻，全公司会真正 rally 在后面。那是那种能阶跃式改变我们产品市场匹配的东西，我们会在它后面做一堆活动。但同时，对我们重要的是维持市场上的"噪音"。而那噪音，靠我们每天、隔天、一天多次地发布、并持续聊它而发生。有趣的是，它其实是个极棒的"复活"策略，因为人们会想"哦，这儿又有新东西了，我得去瞧瞧"。它也是个极棒的再参与策略。所以与其发简报说"这是市场趋势、这是用户故事"，人们是真的登进社媒看"好，Lovable 现在又发了什么？"——"变了啥？"对他们来说看这个很有意思，因为从他们说出"需要什么"到实际交付，间隔极短，所以他们觉得自己被听到了。而且他们确实被听到了，因为我们就是那么排优先级的。但有趣的是，我从没待过一家试图维持这么多发布速度、来维持一定噪音、让人觉得产品是"活"的公司。它每周都在变。然后还有那些大的放大、赛车模型里说的 turbo boost，出去后从根本上对整体产品市场匹配造出阶跃式改变。而那是种我天天都认同的留存策略。我只希望我们继续扩时还能维持它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sounds stressful. This reminds me, I had a... Gaurav, he's the CEO of Mirage. Used to be called Captions, which is a really successful AI video company startup. And they have a policy of you ship a marketable feature every week. That's how their company operates. And it's the same thing, it's just ship things you can talk about.
turns.zh: 听起来压力山大。这让我想起，我有个……Gaurav，他是 Mirage 的 CEO。以前叫 Captions，一家很成功的 AI 视频创业公司。他们有个政策：每周发一个能拿来讲的功能。他们公司就这么运作。一样的，就是发那些你能拿来讲的东西。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Velocity of shipping is our number one core value in development team. So we do anything and everything to just keep it going up, up, up and into the right. And by the way, this also means that everybody has a little bit of marketer within them. We have very lean product organization. We actually lean on our engineers to do a lot of product work. We call them product engineers, and they have to go and they have to announce the thing that they've shipped. It doesn't just funnel through marketing. (00:27:57): So there is a lot of autonomy, a lot of agency that needs to happen with this type of velocity. Because otherwise, you have to have enormous marketing team to staff that. So it has to come with some roles and responsibilities. Redefinition on the team as well.
turns.zh: 发布速度是我们开发团队头号核心价值观。所以我们做一切让它就一路向上、向右。顺便说，这也意味着每个人身上都有点市场人。我们产品组织极精简。我们其实靠工程师做很多产品工作。我们叫他们产品工程师，他们得去宣布自己发了的东西。它不流经市场部。所以要维持这种速度，需要很多自主、很多能动性。否则你得有个巨型市场团队去撑。所以它得配上一些角色和职责的重新定义。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's talk about marketing. That's something else you've written about is just marketing is changing in a big way, their role in growth. How does marketing play a role in all of this?
turns.zh: 我们聊聊市场。这是你写过的另一件事——市场正在大变，它在增长里的角色在变。市场在整个里面扮演什么角色？

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: On one side, marketing channels are changing. On the other side, marketing's involvement into everything that product does is changing. And then number three, I think even marketing organizations in terms of where they hire the most are changing as a result as well. So I'll talk about second one first, just because we just talked about shipping, and that is... Yeah, you still have your product marketers, you still have your channel managers. But they focus more on the big things and the narratives. (00:28:49): Although it's difficult, because the narrative even changes all the time. As these functionalities come through, usually you can come up with a positioning and messaging, and you can have it for years and create all of the campaigns around it. Now, you have it for three months, and then the product changes. So the cycles here are really, really short. And for smaller changes, because cycles are so short, they spend so much time actually focusing on it as they should. (00:29:15): But some of these smaller changes just cannot be supported by marketing. You have to delegate it to your product and engineering team to do their own marketing, because otherwise, again, you'd have to have an enormous marketing team in order to support it all. (00:29:27): But at the same time, channels in which marketing right now works I think are changing quite a bit. And not enough people I feel like are freaking out and talking about it, as opposed to moving just in the same direction over and over again. And the changes that I'm seeing is that it has been very clear to me that when you're talking about marketing organic strategy, if you asked me that five years ago, I would've said that's SEO. It's search engine optimization. Go on Google, that's your organic marketing strategy. (00:29:58): If you ask me what's your organic marketing strategy right now, to me it's all about social. Which is what is my CEO posting? What is my team posting? What is my creator economy doing? Influencer marketing, and across all of the social platforms. That is my organic, which is... That one's paid, to be fair. But when I think about organic, there is still a lot of that word of mouth. What are my users posting on social? What are they talking about it? What are they sharing? (00:30:26): Which is a mind shift, because I've been always... Especially in B2B, so focused on search. And now I feel like it's been completely pushed even further into consumerization territory, and it has become all about social no matter how B2B you are, because that's where eyeballs are at.
turns.zh: 一方面，市场渠道在变。另一方面，市场对产品所做一切事情的参与度在变。第三，我觉得连市场组织最常招人的方向也在随之变。我先聊第二个，因为刚聊完发布，也就是……对，你还是有产品经理、还是有渠道经理。但他们更聚焦在大事和叙事上。虽然这很难，因为连叙事都在一直变。随着这些功能出来，通常你能定个位和话术，用几年、围绕它做所有战役。现在你只能撑三个月，然后产品就变了。所以这里的周期真的极短。而对小改动，因为周期这么短，他们花大量时间聚焦在上面——本该如此。但有些小改动市场根本撑不住。你得把它委派给你的产品和工程团队，让他们自己做营销，否则你又得有个巨型市场团队才能撑住所有。但同时，市场现在运作的渠道，我觉得变了不少。而且我觉得没足够多的人在慌、在聊这个，反而一味往同一个方向走。我看到的改变很明确：说到自然增长策略，如果你五年前问我，我会说那是 SEO，搜索引擎优化，上 Google，那就是你的自然增长策略。如果你现在问我自然增长策略是什么，对我来说是全关于社媒。也就是我的 CEO 在发什么？我的团队在发什么？我的创作者经济在干嘛？网红营销，跨所有社媒平台。那是我的"自然"——不过那个其实是付费的，老实说。但说到自然，还是有很多口碑。我的用户在社媒上发什么？他们在聊什么？在分享什么？这是种思维转变，因为我一直……尤其在 B2B，那么聚焦搜索。现在我觉得它被进一步推进了消费化的地界，已经全关于社媒、不管你多 B2B，因为眼球在那儿。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is fascinating. And so when you talk about socials, what are you finding is most helpful? Is it Twitter/X? Is it LinkedIn? Is it YouTube, TikTok, Instagram?
turns.zh: 太有意思了。所以说到社媒，你发现什么最有用的？是 Twitter/X？LinkedIn？YouTube、TikTok、Instagram？

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: For founder socials, our employee socials, X and LinkedIn are fantastic sources. Especially for B2B, because that's where all of the BBWB people are at. But you cannot just have ChatGPT write your copy and post it, you need to show personality. There needs to be humanity that it goes through it. And it's not natural for everybody, and it feels very awkward sometimes to start. But it's important to people to see who is building the company, because there's so much competition now on functionality, so they can rally behind a team. (00:31:28): So they want to have a team that they want to win. And for that, you need to be vulnerable, you need to be authentic, obviously, but you just need to be yourself. That corporate scrubbing has to completely fall off, which is obviously going to pull in as the company scales. But at least at the beginning, that is your chance to stand out. (00:31:52): And then your customers posting about you. So that word of mouth of really creating a product that creates something for customers that is worth talking about. It gives them stories that they want to share, that feels empowering to them to tell to others like they're unlocking a secret. They feel proud of what they have created. (00:32:14): Which what we focus a lot on, Lovable on, to have that feeling of, "Oh my gosh, I have superpowers now and I can't wait to tell others. I cannot wait to show others what is happening." So on both of those sides, to me, that is very much organic. If you aren't a consumer, then Instagram, TikTok are very much a go as well.
turns.zh: 对创始人社媒、对我们员工社媒，X 和 LinkedIn 是极棒的来源。尤其对 B2B，因为所有 B2B 的人都在那。但你不能就让 ChatGPT 写文案发上去，你得展现个性。得有人味儿流过它。这对不是每个人都自然，有时候开头很尴尬。但对人们来说，看到谁在建这家公司很重要，因为现在功能上的竞争太多了，他们能 rally 在一个团队后面。他们想要一个他们希望赢的团队。为此你得脆弱、得真实，当然，但你只要做自己。那种公司打磨感得彻底掉，而随着公司扩大那显然会回来。但至少在初期，那是你脱颖而出的机会。然后是你客户替你发。所以那种口碑——真正造出一个给用户、值得拿来聊的产品。它给他们想分享的故事，让他们觉得像在解锁秘密、告诉别人很有力量。他们对自己造出来的东西感到骄傲。这恰是我们 Lovable 重点关注的，去营造那种"天呐我现在有超能力了、等不及要告诉别人、等不及要展示给别人看"的感觉。所以在这两边，对我来说是极强的自然增长。如果你不是消费产品，那 Instagram、TikTok 也完全能上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The CEO clearly is an important variable in this, them. In this case, Anton just tweeting, "Here's what's going on Lovable. Here's how fast it's growing. He's something we've learned."
turns.zh: CEO 显然是个重要变量。在这个案例里，Anton 就发推"Lovable 最近怎么样。我们增长多快。这是我们学到的东西。"

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: It is.
turns.zh: 正是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We had the CEO of Gamma on recently, granted, and he's exactly the same thing. Just sharing a bunch of lessons, journey building in public, a big part of the growth lever. And your point here is okay, so it's the CEO. But then it's also how do you get your customers to share things on socials? And then there's a paid influencer component.
turns.zh: 我们最近请了 Gamma 的 CEO，说真的，他一模一样。就是分享一堆经验教训、公开构建的旅程，是增长杠杆的大头。而你的点是：好，所以是 CEO。但然后还有你怎么让客户在社媒上分享？然后还有付费网红这一块。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yes, the customer is difficult one. That's a word of mouth loop that you need to stand up. The only way to create a word of mouth loop is just to blow their socks off when they actually experience your product. We have a almost unfair advantage, because our product is called Lovable. So by default, we're trying to create absolute lovable experiences. That is a mentality internally. If it's not lovable, we're not going to ship it. And the best way to fix a bug at Lovable is to say, "This is not lovable," and everybody just jumps on it to fix it right there and then. Sprints, no sprints, it doesn't matter, it's getting fixed right now. (00:33:40): So from that perspective, we have that culture already embedded as part of our brand and it's part of our name which helps us a lot. But the point is that you feel that brand through every interaction. I talk to my designer all the time, how can we add more love marks into the product? How can we prioritize more unique interactions? The little elements that make up that feeling of this product is speaking to me. It's like, "It feels something that is unique." It has personality behind it. (00:34:08): So we put all of the brand work actually into our product. When you think about Lovable, people think about a brand, but we don't have a brand marketing team yet. So it's all just through product interactions, and some of those building and public moments of the people behind those product interactions that is our strategy. (00:34:28): And then there's influencer marketing. Interestingly enough, influencer marketing is 10 times bigger for us than paid social. So yeah, we do some paid social as well, and it's working decently. It's quite expensive from payback period, we're still optimizing it. As I said, we're pretty early on in all of these channels. But influencer marketing is something that has worked from the beginning at Lovable. And a reason behind it is that influencer marketing, especially on the socials, it gives you an opportunity to have a little video and interaction. And Lovable is all about seeing like, "Oh my gosh, this is what I can do, and this is possible." So that drives people to go and try it themselves. (00:35:07): So that's why social works very well for us, because it's not really a written value proposition. Nobody knows what vibe coding is. But you watch 10 seconds of it and you go, "Whew, that's new. Let me go give it a try."
turns.zh: 对，客户那块难。那是你需要立起来的口碑循环。要造出口碑循环，唯一的办法就是在他们真正体验你产品时把他们的袜子惊掉。我们有个近乎不公平的优势，因为我们的产品叫 Lovable。所以默认地，我们在试图造绝对 lovable 的体验。那是内部的一种心态。如果它不可爱，我们就不发。在 Lovable 修 bug 最好的方式就是说"这不可爱"，然后所有人立刻扑上去当场修。有 sprint 没 sprint 无所谓，现在就修。所以从那个角度，那种文化已经嵌进我们的品牌、也是我们名字的一部分，帮了我们大忙。但重点是你在每次互动里都能感受到那个品牌。我总跟我的设计师聊，我们怎么往产品里加更多"爱的印记"？怎么优先更多独特的互动？那些构成"这产品在跟我说话"感觉的小元素。它让人觉得"这东西是独特的"，背后有人格。所以我们把所有的品牌工作其实都放进了产品里。你想到 Lovable，人们想到一个品牌，但我们还没有品牌市场团队。所以全靠产品互动，以及那些产品互动背后的人公开构建的时刻——那就是我们的策略。然后还有网红营销。有趣的是，网红营销对我们来说是付费社媒的 10 倍大。所以我们也做点付费社媒，效果还行。回收周期挺贵，我们还在优化。如我所言，我们在所有这些渠道都还早。但网红营销是从 Lovable 一开始就奏效的。背后的原因是，网红营销、尤其在社媒上，给你机会放个小视频和互动。而 Lovable 全关于"看到"——"天呐，这是我又能做的、这是可能的"。所以它驱动人们自己去试。所以社媒对我们特别好，因为它其实不是书面的价值主张。没人有概念 vibe coding 是什么。但你看了 10 秒，你就"哇，那是新的。让我去试试。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Who would've thought that a head of growth, who is traditionally seen as data, metrics, spreadsheets, drive KPIs is like, "Okay, how do we make this more lovable? How do we add more moments of delight?"
turns.zh: 谁能想到一个传统上被视为数据、指标、表格、驱动 KPI 的增长负责人，会像"好，我们怎么让它更可爱？我们怎么加更多惊喜时刻？"

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: I know. My joke is at the end of my Lovable journey whenever... Hopefully it never comes to an end. But at the end I'll be a growth brand person. Hi, my name is Elena, I do brand now. But I actually see it as part of growth strategy to make sure that that brand shines through every single interaction. And I always talk to my team about it, because that is one big lever in our growth story.
turns.zh: 我知道。我的玩笑是，在我 Lovable 旅程的终点——希望它永不到来——我会是个增长品牌人。嗨，我是 Elena，我现在做品牌。但我其实把它看作增长战略的一部分，确保那个品牌在每次互动里都闪光。我总跟团队聊这个，因为那是我们增长故事里一个大杠杆。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, so I think that's a really important point to highlight. The reason Lovable is growing so fast is it is a product people love. You've made something people want. And the word of mouth spreads, because it's something that blows people's socks off as you said. So it feels like that's the first thing you got to get right.
turns.zh: 对，所以我觉得那是个真该强调的重点。Lovable 长得这么快，是因为它是人们爱的产品。你做出了人们想要的东西。口碑传开，因为它像你说的，把人的袜子都惊掉了。所以感觉那是你首先得搞对的事。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yes. Well, the first thing you have to get right is you have to be at the right place at the right time and you have to be in fast moving waters. Let's not discount how fast this category is exploding on its own. So this cannot happen in every single category that you're starting to build a product. But the way to stand out in the super crowded category is to create experiences that speak to people. (00:36:33): That I think is something that a lot of people deprioritize, because they still prioritize functionality over humanity within software. And I think that we're actually moving to the new era of software that needs to feel human, that people want to interact with, not just utility of it. Because cost of software is coming down so much to develop that we now can actually invest into emotional feel of that software, as opposed to only just focus on creating the utility out of it. (00:37:04): So to me, it's a... I love this move, because I hate nothing more than going to software that is just so painful to use that I lose some brain cells as I'm interacting with it, versus software that I feel I get energy out of. And for Lovable for me, I cannot wait on some of the projects that I have to go and vibe code myself. That's the highlight of my day. I bring in my daughter and I'm like, "Let's go do this." Like, "What do you think that needs to be done?" Because I just get so much energy out of doing it. And that is the feeling you cannot create by looking at it as a utility problem.
turns.zh: 对。你首先得搞对的，是得在正确的地点、正确的时间，得处在湍急的水里。别小看这个品类自己爆炸得多快。所以这不会发生在你正起步做的每一个品类。但在极度拥挤的品类里脱颖而出的方式，是造出会和人"说话"的体验。我觉得很多人把它排低优先级，因为他们还把功能放在软件里的人味儿之上。而我觉得我们其实在走向软件的新纪元——它需要感觉人性化、是人们想互动的，而不只是它的实用性。因为软件开发成本降得这么多，我们现在真能往软件的情感质感上投，而不只聚焦造出它的实用性。所以对我而言，这是……我爱这个转向，因为我最恨的莫过于用那种痛苦到交互时都掉脑细胞的软件，而不是用那种让我获得能量的软件。对 Lovable 来说，我等不及去做我手上一些项目、自己去 vibe code。那是我一天的高光。我把女儿带过来，我说"我们去做这个"，"你觉得需要做什么？"因为我从中获得太多能量。而那种感觉，你是没法把它当实用性问题去造出来的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The way I think about it, the way what you're describing is it's almost table stakes have increased, and now it's so easy to build. Now the big differentiator is experience, design, delight.
turns.zh: 我的理解是，你说的几乎等于"赌注门槛"提高了，现在造东西太容易了。现在最大的差异化是体验、设计、惊喜感。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Exactly, and it has to translate through every single interaction. So your designer has to be one of your first hires now in startups. It's not just about the engineering, so to speak, utility. And you have to think through every single interaction of, does this communicate our brand or not?
turns.zh: 正是，而且它得在每一次互动里都体现出来。所以你的设计师现在得是创业公司最早招的人之一。不只是工程、也就是实用性。你得想清楚每一次互动：这到底有没有传达我们的品牌？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So along those lines, I want to come back to something you talked about, which is launching new features as a huge growth lever. The big question there is just how do you maintain quality and cohesiveness as all these people are empowered to ship stuff? Is there anything else there you've seen that works well to help avoid just the Frankenstein product that's endless features that you want to tweet about?
turns.zh: 顺着这个，我想回到你聊过的一点——把发新功能当成一个巨大的增长杠杆。那里的大问题是：当所有这些人都被赋能去发布东西，你怎么维持质量和一致性？你有没有看到什么别的做法，能帮着避免造出一个 Frankenstein 产品——无穷的功能、你却想拿它发推？

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yeah. One part of it is not something that you can codify, but it's the type of people that you hire that are going to go and ship these things. We at Lovable try to hire the absolute best talent available out there that we can bring in, and that we can source and that we can attract to grow with. And what do I mean by that best talent? It's not that somebody who has been at really large companies, or somebody that has really done a lot of logos or has big success stories behind them. It's somebody who is extremely passionate about their job. (00:38:59): It's their hobby. They love to work. They have fire in their belly. This is not a paycheck for them, they want to do this for some ulterior reason. This is the biggest opportunity of their life, so this is global maximum against any other opportunities that are in front of them at the moment. So that's very important for us. (00:39:18): We want people to come and do their absolute best work at Lovable. It's very important, and you can feel it in this office. People are wired up. They are so high on how can we make this better? How can we deliver more to our customers? And that's very different compared to usually how companies grow where like, "Okay, yeah, the check, check, check. They fit the skillset, let's bring them in." But is that passion, is that fire behind it? (00:39:45): And then the second piece is that we work really hard on just addressing what's the success here looks like? What is it that we're building? What use cases are we building for? And then because we hire these people that are so passionate about it, the other two skills, by the way, that are super important is high agency and high autonomy. I can figure out things that are tangential to me that I don't need other specialties, so to speak. I don't need a marketer to go launch something, I can go figure it out. And I have high agency, I can go do it myself. I'm going to own it all the way from start to finish. Those are very important, something that we screen for and something that we look for in our culture. (00:40:25): And then you just see... What you want to do is up to you. So there's very little supervision that happens on the ground. Now, we all have goals and some of the big launches that we're all marching towards, but some of the work that is completely up to developers, up to marketers or whatever, what is it that they want to do? So there has to be that enablement of go try things. And because of our velocity, if you fail, it's not a big deal. We'll just pivot, we will get through it. We are not here to just win all the time.
