turns.en: Another one is giving your product away a lot. And for AI products, it may feel counterintuitive because they're so costly. Every single interaction with an AI product costs companies something. There's an LLM pass-through cost that is coming through. And a lot of, especially traditional tech companies I see are gating AI immediately behind the paywall because they're sitting on a really cush, high margin profile, and the moment that you start giving AI away for free, you're cutting into those margins like a knife through the butter. Now, at the same time, AI being so new and the capabilities being so new, you have to remove the barrier of entry. You have to give a lot of your product away for free. But by the way, I don't just mean freemium. Freemium to me is just a baseline. If you're in the new category, you need to let people explore what it is free and get that initial wow moment. (00:52:48): It's not aha moment, by the way. It doesn't need to be aha moment anymore. It just needs to be a wow moment. And for Lovable, it's that first preview generation after your first prompt, even though it's absolutely not going to be complete thing of what you want to build, but you just go, "This is possible? I had no idea. I want to keep building." And it becomes an addictive exercise. (00:53:08): But we also give so many of our Lovable credits away to every event, to every hackathon. If you want to host a Lovable hackathon, we will sponsor it and give all of the participants credits away for free. We give them away as candy and we basically track them over our LLM costs on freemium and giveaways as our marketing costs, and it doesn't go into our something we need to reduce to make our margins better. It goes into, this is something that we need to spend more in because this is part of our growth secret sauce.
turns.zh: 另一个是把产品大量送出去。对 AI 产品来说，这听起来反直觉，因为它们成本太高了。每一次 AI 互动都会让公司付出代价——有 LLM 的转嫁成本。我看到很多尤其是传统科技公司，马上就把 AI 挡在付费墙后面，因为他们习惯了超高的利润率，一旦免费送 AI，利润就像热刀切黄油一样被削掉。但与此同时，AI 这么新、能力这么新，你必须降低进入门槛，得大量免费送。不过我说的不仅是 freemium，freemium 对我来说是基本线。如果你在一个新品类里，你得让人免费去探索、获得最初的 wow 时刻。这已经不是 aha 时刻了，不需要 aha，只要 wow 就够了。对 Lovable 来说，就是第一次提示之后生成的第一个预览——虽然它肯定不是你想要的完整成品，但你会"这居然能行？我之前完全不知道，我还想继续做"。这就变成了上瘾的过程。我们还把大量 Lovable 额度送给每个活动、每个黑客松。你想办 Lovable 黑客松，我们赞助，给所有参与者免费额度。我们像发糖一样送，把 freemium 和赠送产生的 LLM 成本当成营销成本来算，它不是那种"为了提升利润率要削减"的开支，而是"我们得花更多"的开支，因为这是我们增长的秘密配方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, I want to hear more about the growth secret sauce. That is extremely interesting. I haven't heard of that as a strategy, and I can see why this makes sense. If the strategy is blow people's socks off so they can tell their friends, post on all socials, the trick is get more people to try it. And it's such a new, crazy thing. Why would I pay money? Why would I even go take the effort to try sign up for an account? I don't know what this is. I don't know what I'm doing with it. So I could see how this loop goes faster and faster by giving it away.
turns.zh: 好，我想多听听这个增长秘密配方。太有意思了，我从没听过这种策略，但我能理解为什么行得通。如果策略是让人惊掉下巴好去告诉朋友、发到所有社交平台，那关键就是让更多人去试。而这东西又新又疯狂，我凭什么付钱？我凭什么费劲去注册账号？我都不知道这是啥、能用它干嘛。所以我能理解，免费送能让这个循环转得越来越快。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Exactly. And again, this is very uncomfortable sometimes for companies that A, either used to really... AI companies have lower profile of margins. That's absolutely true. To find an AI company with 80%, 90% margin profile is absolutely impossible, let's be real. We're all sitting somewhere in a 40% or so, which is a lot smaller. So any time that you look at those AI costs as your cost center, that's when you're in trouble. You fundamentally have to flip the script and say, "I need to expose to people of what is possible and I need to remove the monetization friction out of it." Because if you don't, nobody's ever going to try it, or you're going to be very easily overtaken by a competitor that will give it away. And let's face it, once you hook people, they're more likely going to stay with you. So you obviously have to still work on the retention strategy there. (00:54:59): But if you can have, like for our case, if somebody, one of our users stands up and say, "Hey, I'm going to have a hackathon at my work on Lovable. Can you give us all some free credits to play with?" Why would we prevent a person who wants to do all of the marketing and activating job for us in their company from using us? (00:55:21): Of course, we're like, "Take it. How much do you need? How much would you like? We will sponsor it all. We will give you anything that you need." So we're really leaning into people that are wanting to show this magic to those around you and empowering them as much as possible. And that is something that is actually applies to every single product. And I agree, this is not a growth strategy that I've ever applied in my life on giving product away as much as possible, but it is something that is more and more becoming something that I see that is absolutely non-negotiable.
turns.zh: 没错。而且这对一些公司来说很难受，要么是习惯了……AI 公司的利润率本来就低，这是事实。想找个 80%、90% 利润率的 AI 公司基本不可能，现实点说，大家都落在 40% 左右，小很多。所以只要你把 AI 成本当成成本中心，你就麻烦了。你必须彻底反转思路，说"我得让人看到什么是可能的，把变现摩擦拿掉"。因为不这么做，没人会试，或者你很容易被一个免费送的对手干掉。而且说实话，一旦你钩住了人，他们更可能留下来。所以你显然还得做留存。但像我们的情况，如果有个用户站起来说"嘿，我要在公司办个 Lovable 黑客松，能给我们点免费额度玩玩吗？"我们凭什么去阻止一个愿意在公司里帮我们做营销和激活的人？当然就是"拿去，要多少？尽管说，我们全包，你要多少给多少"。所以我们特别扶持那些想把这魔法展示给身边人的人，尽可能赋能他们。这件事其实适用于所有产品。我承认，我这辈子从没用过"尽可能送产品"这种增长策略，但现在我看到这越来越变成一种绝对的刚需。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I'm feeling is the more mind-blowing it is, the more you should give it away for free.
turns.zh: 我的感觉是，越让人惊掉下巴，就越该免费送。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Especially in a competitive market where everyone is... It's hard. There's so many companies trying to do this thing, and so it's almost like the better you are, the more you should give it away.
turns.zh: 尤其是在竞争激烈的市场里，大家都在……很难，这么多公司都在做这事，所以几乎是你越厉害，越该免费送。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this also explains why so much VC money has to be raised for these sorts of companies because this is not cheap. Like you said, you're paying all these foundational models a lot of money.
turns.zh: 这也解释了为什么这类公司得融那么多 VC 钱，因为这不便宜。就像你说的，你给那些基础模型付了很多钱。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yes and no. I'm only going to say no is because, so take a look at Lovable, we're over 200 million in ARR. At this point, we're 100 people large so our headcount costs are very low.
turns.zh: 是也不是。我说不，是因为你看 Lovable，我们现在 ARR 超过 2 亿了。目前我们 100 人，所以人力成本很低。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wait, let me just make sure people hear that. 200 million ARR, I didn't realize 100 people work at Lovable.
turns.zh: 等等，我得确保大家听到这个。2 亿 ARR，我都不知道 Lovable 有 100 人。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yes. And six months ago, we had 30 people working at Lovable so we triple. So for us, it's a really big deal. We tripled our company size.
turns.zh: 对。六个月前我们才 30 人，所以翻了三倍。对我们来说这是个大事，公司规模翻了三倍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such a big company now.
turns.zh: 现在是好大一家公司了。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: We're going to quadruple it by the end of, yeah, I know. We're big boy and girls now. But for perspective of the headcount costs, it's minimal. We have very little in that going on. We are not spending a lot on paid marketing so we're not a big paid marketing driver. Yeah, we're spending on influencer marketing, but it's not majority of our growth. It's low double digits to be fair because it's not why we're successful. It's amplifying our success and it's helping us reach new audiences. We don't have really large sales team, we have only a couple sales folks, and they're just starting to ramp up their enterprise efforts so we don't have really big enterprise demand gen costs as well. (00:57:24): From that perspective, if you look at the equation and you say, "Well, okay, if you're not going to do a lot of paid marketing, if you're not going to do a lot of sales, because we're really only working on hand raisers of people that are saying right now that they want to buy Lovable, then whereas you don't have big costs, so you can spend it on product." (00:57:42): That is the beautiful part because when we are giving our product away to our customers, we're not competing with other companies in that space, because they're just going to use Lovable in their hackathon. We're on their own, and we're not competing on AdWords or in paid Google where everybody's buying real estate for eyeballs. From that perspective, I think about it more as a shift of where we spend in costs. And honestly, it's more efficient way to do paid marketing almost in a sense because of the cost per eyeball that we get there is quite a bit lower compared to if we were trying to compete it on Google. So yes and no to your statement because it actually does not deteriorate margin profile. We're just shifting of where we're spending it.
turns.zh: 到年底我们要翻四倍，是啊我知道，我们现在是大孩子了。但从人力成本角度看，它微不足道，我们在那上面花很少。我们没在付费营销上花很多，所以不是靠大笔付费营销驱动。对，我们投了网红营销，但它不是增长的大头，说实话是低两位数百分比，因为那不是我们成功的原因，它只是放大成功、帮我们触达新人群。我们没有很大的销售团队，就几个销售，他们才刚开始做企业端的努力，所以我们也没有很大的企业需求生成成本。从那个角度看，如果你看这个等式，说"好吧，如果你不做大量付费营销、不做大量销售，因为我们只做那些主动说现在就想买 Lovable 的人的生意，那你就没有大笔成本，所以可以把钱花在产品上"。这一点很美，因为当我们把产品送出去的时候，我们不是在跟那个领域的其他公司竞争，因为他们就是会在自己的黑客松里用 Lovable，我们是独立的一方，不在 AdWords 或付费 Google 上跟所有人抢眼球。从那个角度，我更把它看成花钱位置的转移。老实说，这几乎是更高效的付费营销，因为我们在那拿到的每眼成本比在 Google 上竞争低不少。所以对你的说法我是"是也不是"，因为它其实没有恶化利润率，我们只是转移了花钱的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is an incredibly important point you're making there. It's not like you're generating an incredible amount of revenue, so there is money available to spend. And what you're saying is because it's been spreading through word of mouth mostly, you're not spending tons of money on salespeople, you're not spending tons of money on paid ads. This is just an amazing way to get more people to use it, so it's like a marketing cost.
turns.zh: 你这个观点太关键了。不是说你在疯狂产生收入所以有钱花。你说的是，因为它主要靠口碑传播，你没在销售上砸钱、没在付费广告上砸钱。这只是一个让人更多使用的绝妙方式，就像营销成本。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: This is product-led growth.
turns.zh: 这就是产品驱动增长（product-led growth）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Supercharge.
turns.zh: 超级加强版。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: To the max, supercharged. Yes, because you're literally using your product to drive that awareness by giving it away to the agents in your ecosystem that will do that distribution for you.
turns.zh: 拉满，超级加强。对，因为你真的是在用你的产品去驱动认知，把它送给生态里那些会帮你做分发的 agent。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So fascinating. What a wild world we're living in. Free stuff for everyone.
turns.zh: 太有意思了。我们活在一个多疯狂的世界。人人有免费的东西。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yes. I mean, it's great for consumers. This is a great time to be a consumer. You have so many options. Everybody's throwing themselves at you, giving your product away for free so it's great to be in the market right now. I think the power should be with consumer always, but with software, power has not been with consumer previously because we were forced to use towards some solutions because of either how they were chosen for us or what was available in the market. And now that supply is almost infinite, the demand from the consumers can be very picky and the one that serves the best will win.
turns.zh: 对。对消费者来说是好事，现在当消费者太爽了。你有这么多选择，大家都往你身上扑，免费送产品，所以现在在市场上是好时候。我觉得权力一直就该在消费者手里，但软件界以前权力不在消费者手里，因为要么是别人替我们选了方案，要么是市场上只有那些可选。现在供给几乎无限，消费者的需求可以很挑剔，服务最好的人会赢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think again, it's important to highlight. This is not some kind of VC subsidized bubble-ish sort of thing. There is a lot of money being generated that you are spending to help it grow faster. It's not some kind of, we're just raising more money to give away more money. You're actually making your own money. It's not driven by VC money. Obviously, it helps.
turns.zh: 而且我觉得再强调一遍很重要：这不是某种 VC 补贴出来的泡沫。你是在产生大量收入，然后把它花在加速增长上。不是那种"我们再融资来送更多钱"。你其实是在赚自己的钱，不是靠 VC 钱驱动的。当然，它有帮助。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: I can't comment on specific margin details for us, but at the same time, the money that we're raising on VC is for future development and hardening our business, not because we will not be able to survive without it.
turns.zh: 我没法评论我们具体的利润细节，但与此同时，我们融的 VC 钱是用在后续开发和夯实业务上，不是因为我们没它就活不下去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, great segue too. I want to talk about product-market fit in competition. You have this really interesting post that I don't think people grasp yet, which is that product-market fit is no longer this, we've done it. Product-market fit and we're up into the right. Now we just grow, go, grow. Now we hire salespeople, it's going to be great. You've written that just product-market fit is no longer this like you've done it and you're good. It's this endless fight to keep it. Talk about what you're seeing there.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好，这个过渡也很自然。我想聊聊竞争中的产品市场契合（product-market fit）。你写过一篇很有意思的帖子，我觉得大家还没真正理解——那就是产品市场契合不再是"我们做到了，搞定"，然后一路向右上角，接下来就是招销售、增长、起飞。你写过，产品市场契合不再是"做到了就万事大吉"，而是一种需要不断維持的无尽战斗。讲讲你看到的这个变化。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: I'll first start with what I've felt at least before when people were talking about product-market fit, that yeah, obviously always product-market fit is an evolving thing, but the rate of that evolution was measured in years. What is it that you need the next product-market fit step function change, which often was called second horizon or third horizon. Sometimes five, 10 years, sometimes even longer that you'd need, depending on how good and hard your initial product-market fit was, but you'd spend years scaling the original product-market fit. It was like blitz growth stage. Marketing, sales, growth was very important that you just try to get it to as many people as possible. And then once you have saturation or the cost to getting to the marginal people becomes too high, you start thinking, "Okay, what else can I offer to help me reach additional people or sell more to existing users that I already have?" (01:01:39): And again, the main point here is it would take years to get to that stage where it became a question that you had to face really hard face-to-face. Now, it's three months, and all of a sudden you have to face that question again. And it's happening because of two things, in my opinion. Number one, in AI technology of what LLM is capable of doing changes still very rapidly with new model release, with each new model release. I think we'll stabilize at some point and then it's going to become more marginal, but we're not there yet. So every three months or so, every single AI LLM provider creates a step function change in what is possible with that LLM. And when you have this new possibility in just an underlying technology that opens up in front of you, then it creates another ceiling of what is possible to build on top of it. (01:02:36): The tricky piece here is that it's not enough to just wait for that technology to get better and then start building on top. You have to build beforehand to make a bet and then it's the LLM to catch up because when that model releases, you already need to have that functionality available. That piece is, I've never been in a company where the fundamental capabilities are still changing so rapidly, and that's the product part. The product can leap to the new expectations, but let's not talk about the market part as well. Consumer expectations have never changed this fast before. What we expected ChatGPT to be able to do and answer and how we wanted it to talk to us eight months ago versus now is night and day and the deep thinking mode, and how deeply you can go into answering questions and what is capable of building on top of it. (01:03:31): Consumer perception has never changed this fast too. It's this unprecedented time of consumers all of a sudden in a month saying, "Oh, it's not doing this yet. I'm bouncing." (01:03:43): Before, again, consumer perceptions would be years to take. It's actually technology would sometimes be able to already address it, but consumer perception has not been changed yet so it would take a long time. We're in this really weird part where both product and market is shifting so rapidly that every three months, I feel like we have to recapture our product-market fit and not just recapture on the same technology and with same customers. It's both of those pieces of the equation change every three months, and it's terrifying in a way. It's also very confusing in a way because we're $200 million company, and we're not solely focused on marketing and sales because we still have to recapture our product-market fit. (01:04:26): You know that the team that finds your product-market fit is very different than the team that usually scales your company, yet we have to find the team that is capable of doing both on ongoing basis. Now, I think every AI company is on this product-market fit treadmill. Hopefully that treadmill speed slows down. If not, I think we're going to come up with crazy things of what this LLM and AI will be able to do if it's going to continue at this cusp, but it's a weird place to be in because every three months we have to throttle on our scaling efforts and just reinvent and then scale again. But it's like short blitz of growth, not these long year long commitments.
turns.zh: 我先从过去的感受说起。以前大家聊产品市场契合，当然它一直是个演进中的东西，但那个演进的速度是以"年"来衡量的。你下一次性价比跃迁式的产品市场契合改变，常被称为第二、第三增长曲线，有时候要五到十年，甚至更久，取决于你最初的产品市场契合做得多好、多难。你会花好几年去放大最初的产品市场契合，那是闪电式增长阶段，营销、销售、增长都极其重要，你就是想把它触达尽可能多的人。等到饱和了，或者触达边际用户的成本太高了，你才开始想"好吧，我还能提供什么，去触达更多人或向现有用户卖更多？"关键点是，以前要花好几年才会走到那个必须正面硬刚的阶段。现在，是三个月，你突然又得面对那个问题了。在我看来，这是因为两件事。第一，AI 技术、LLM 能做到的事，随着每个新模型发布仍在快速变化。我觉得某个时点会稳定下来、变得边际化，但还没到。所以大概每三个月，每个 LLM 提供商都会带来一次"什么是可能的"的阶跃式改变。当底层技术在你面前打开这种新可能，它就又给"能在上面构建什么"立了一道新天花板。难的地方在于，光等技术变好再去构建是不够的，你得提前下注去构建，然后等 LLM 追上来——因为等模型发布了，你得已经把那个功能准备好了。这一点我从来没待过一家基础能力还在这么快变化的公司，这是产品那一侧。产品能跳到新期望上，但也别漏了市场那一侧。消费者的期望以前从没变这么快。八个月前我们期待 ChatGPT 能做什么、怎么回答、想让它怎么跟我们说话，跟现在天差地别——深度思考模式、能多深入地回答问题、能在上面构建什么。消费者认知也从没变这么快。这是前所未有的时代，消费者会突然在一个月内说"哦，它这个还做不到，我走了"。以前消费者认知要好几年才变，有时候技术其实已经能解决了，但消费者认知还没跟上，所以要很久。现在我们处在一个很怪的位置：产品和市场的 shifting 都这么快，每三个月我就觉得得重新抓住一次产品市场契合，而且不只是用同样的技术、同样的客户去重抓，等式两边的这两块每三个月都变，某种程度上挺可怕的，也有点令人困惑，因为我们是个 2 亿美元的公司，却没法只专注在营销和销售上，因为我们还得重新抓住产品市场契合。你知道，找到产品市场契合的团队，和通常放大公司规模的团队是很不一样的，可我们得找到一支能持续同时做这两件事的团队。我觉得每家 AI 公司都在这台产品市场契合的跑步机上。希望这台跑步机的速度能慢下来。如果不能，如果它一直保持这个势头，我觉得我们会搞出 LLM 和 AI 能做到的疯狂东西，但这位置确实很怪，因为每三个月我们就得在规模化努力上踩刹车，推倒重来，然后再规模化。但这是短促的闪电式增长，不是那种长达数年的承诺。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What makes this very real is just this week, apparently OpenAI had this whole code red moment where even though OpenAI by far the leading AI assistant over almost a billion, I think monthly active users, basically synonymous with AI around the world, with Gemini 3 launching, their market share just started to dip really quickly. I think they lost six something percent in a week. And so even OpenAI, ChatGPT, the original, the one that everyone uses constantly is in danger.
turns.zh: 让这一切特别真实的是，就这周，OpenAI 显然经历了一次"红色警报"时刻——尽管 OpenAI 到目前为止是遥遥领先的 AI 助手，差不多有十亿月活，基本是全世界 AI 的代名词，但随着 Gemini 3 发布，他们的市场份额开始快速下滑。我觉得他们一周内就掉了六个多百分点。所以连 OpenAI、ChatGPT，这个最原始、大家每天都在用的东西，都处在危险中。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: It's like nobody's future is bulletproof yet. And 10 years ago, if you asked me if a $200 million company was at risk in losing product-market fit in the next three months if it's experiencing 10% month-over-month growth, I would've said, "You're crazy." And now that's the reality that we live in. And I don't know, it's fascinating to world in. What a time to be alive.
turns.zh: 就像现在没人的未来是防弹的。十年前，如果你问我一家月环比增长 10%、2 亿美元的公司，未来三个月有没有可能失去产品市场契合，我会说"你疯了吧"。可现在这就是我们活着的现实。我不知道，活在这个世界里挺迷人的。真是个活着的年代。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Time to be alive and very stressful, but the prize at the end is massive. That's why this is worth doing, not just monetarily, but just the impact it's going to have on the world, the way we people build and ship.
turns.zh: 是个活着的年代，也非常有压力，但终点的奖赏是巨大的。这就是为什么这事值得做，不只为了钱，也为了它将对世界、对我们人们构建和交付方式产生的影响。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Exactly. The ceiling of what is possible has been raised so massively that we haven't even became too closest to even see it, I believe. I think that that's the exciting part of it.
turns.zh: 没错。什么是可能的，这个天花板被抬得太高了，我们甚至还没接近看到它的边。我觉得那才是令人兴奋的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The way I've seen you write about this product-market fit challenge is the traditional approach is you have these core users that are using it happy with it, and then you expand to the adjacent users and expand to the next. You're basically just trying to recapture that same core constantly and don't even have time to go adjacent.
turns.zh: 我看到你写这个产品市场契合挑战的方式是：传统做法是你有一批核心用户在用、用得开心，然后你扩展到相邻用户、再扩展到下一批。你现在基本只是在不断重新抓住同一批核心，连去相邻用户那里的时间都没有。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yeah. Bangaly wrote a really wonderful article. It was many years ago at this point on adjacent user theory in that your product-market fit expansion when you're in no growth stages, the biggest opportunity for you to go after is this what you call the adjacent user, which are just outside of your core user. They have somewhat similar needs, but maybe they're in different geo, maybe they have slightly different use case, slightly different needs. And your biggest way to continue growing a product-market fit without having to go to next horizon is to capture that next group of users. The interesting piece here of how I relate to it, we still have the core users. And by the way, those core users are mostly pioneers right now that are excited by the capabilities. Then there's latent majority that is filled with adjacent users. And the issue right now, which I'm actually quite worried about us as a category is that we're constantly focusing on recapturing the pioneers. (01:07:39): We don't have time to go after adjacent users, and I'm worried of whether there's going to be a gap in the space where we actually going to alienate the latent majority because we're so hyper focused on just staying top of mind and top capabilities on the pioneers. But I don't know the right answer here, because without the pioneers, you need pioneers for latent majority to follow. But if you take pioneers and you take them too far into capabilities, will latent majority never be able to catch up? Maybe this is a fruitless concern, but it's just something that I think about because at this stage we should be working on adjacent users. I would argue maybe OpenAI definitely started to do that with how many people they have on their platform, but not most of the other AI companies.
turns.zh: 对。Bangaly 很多年前写过一篇很棒的文章，讲相邻用户理论——说当你处于非增长阶段时，产品市场契合扩展的最大机会，是去抓你说的"相邻用户"，也就是在你的核心用户之外、需求有点相似但可能在不同的地区、有略微不同的用例或需求的人。在不进入下一增长曲线的情况下，继续做产品市场契合的最大方式，就是抓住下一批用户。我联想到的是，我们仍然有核心用户——而且他们现在大多是那种被能力兴奋到的先驱者，然后是充满相邻用户的潜在多数。我现在真正担心的，是这个品类会一直盯着重新抓住先驱者。我们没时间去抓相邻用户，而我担心的是，会不会出现一个断层——我们因为太专注于在先驱者心里保持 top of mind 和 top 能力，反而把潜在多数给疏远了。但我不知道正确答案是什么，因为没有先驱者，潜在多数就不会跟上来。可如果你把先驱者带得太远、能力太超前，潜在多数会不会永远追不上？也许这是多虑，但这就是我会想的事，因为在这个阶段我们本该在搞相邻用户。我觉得 OpenAI 凭平台上那么多人，肯定开始这么做了，但其他大多数 AI 公司没有。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I completely see what you're thinking there. A brand could just become known as that's just for startups and prototyping and it's not for serious work.
turns.zh: 我完全懂你在想什么。一个品牌可能就变成"那是给创业公司和做原型的，不是干正经活的"。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yeah, or it's for techies. It's for tech people. It never actually enters the people outside of our little bubble that we live in.
turns.zh: 对，或者"那是给技术宅的，给 tech 人的"，它永远进不了我们这个小泡泡之外的人群。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We touched on this a little bit of just working in AI, working on AI companies, challenging, stressful, a lot of work. What's your advice for folks that are thinking about, should I join a Lovable? Should I join a Cursor? Should I-
turns.zh: 我们稍微聊过在 AI 公司工作、做 AI 公司很有挑战、压力大、活儿多。对那些在想"我要不要加入 Lovable？要不要加入 Cursor？要不要……"的人，你有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... are thinking about, "Should I join a Lovable? Should I join a Cursor? Should I just go work at Google?" (01:09:05): Not to throw them under the bus or anything. Although Google, very, very successful in AI now, maybe a less AI-focused company.
turns.zh: ……在想"我要不要加入 Lovable？要不要加入 Cursor？要不要直接去 Google？"——不是要踩它们一脚，不过 Google 现在在 AI 上非常、非常成功，也许是个没那么聚焦 AI 的公司。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: I really believe that there's different... You need to understand what's the environment that is right for you. Just please understand that AI companies are very hectic at the moment. They're very unstable by definition of that product-market fit treadmill, about that distribution of how they're actually distribute to the market, really changing about how product is even being developed in the first place. So if you are very comfortable in being in that messy middle and really comfortable of converting chaos into clarity for you and those around you, then yeah, AI company is a wonderful place for you to really absorb new skill sets right now. Because even before joining Lovable, when I kept seeing AI, I'm like, "My gosh, I'm so tired of seeing AI everywhere. Is it really changing the world? Is it really changing the way people work?" (01:10:02): And I was at Dropbox before, and yeah, we would use AI here and there and I would use ChatGPT. I've never used AI there the way I use AI at Lovable and the things that I'm capable of accomplishing at Lovable, and I don't know if I ever would've made that leap so fast unless I joined Lovable. If I would've just read or listened about it, it's just different compared to be surrounded by people where it's expectation. It's not like a nice-to-have or something that somebody's asking you to do. This is just how you get things done. And you have to think about everything of, "What can AI do here versus where do I add value versus in a traditional sense of work?" because I start with my own value and then I augment it with AI. And here, the mindset has completely shifted. (01:10:47): Now, I don't think AI is replacing everybody's job, so please don't look at it as that cliche saying. I actually often call AI as average intelligence that helps me get the platform up. And then I add my human thinking and my human creativity on top of it to get it to the next level. But at least I can get this base level done with AI really freaking quickly. (01:11:11): So from that perspective, I think if you want to leapfrog on what it means to be AI native employee and how to use all of these AI tools, you should go to AI company. But if you know that your superpower is in more structure and more definition and a really high specialty of things, because in AI companies, they're all fairly small, so you'll have to generalize quite a bit and have a lot of ownership, all of areas that you usually maybe not have ownership over, then you shouldn't join it, because AI companies will evolve to be more stable too. (01:11:43): So it's just a matter of time on where you can join. So I would just urge people to look at their superpowers and the type of environments that really speak to them so they can feel happy, because this can lead to burnout for wrong type of personalities very quickly.
turns.zh: 我真心相信，环境对不对，是因人而异的。只要搞清楚什么样的环境适合你就好。但请理解，AI 公司现在非常混乱。按产品市场契合跑步机的本质，它们天然就不稳定——关于它们到底怎么分销到市场、关于产品最初到底怎么被开发出来，都在剧烈变化。所以如果你很能在那个混乱的中间地带待着，很能把混沌为你和身边人转化成清晰，那 AI 公司对你来说就是个绝佳的地方，能让你现在快速吸收新技能。因为在加入 Lovable 之前，我一直看 AI，就会想"天哪，我太烦到处都是 AI 了。它真在改变世界吗？真在改变人们工作的方式吗？"我之前在 Dropbox，对，我们这里那里会用点 AI，我也会用 ChatGPT。但我从没像在 Lovable 这样用 AI，也从来没在 Lovable 做到过我现在能做到的这些事，我不知道如果我没加入 Lovable，会不会这么快就跨出那一步。如果我只是读读、听听，那跟被一群"这就是预期"的人包围完全不同。这不是 nice-to-have，也不是谁让你做的事，这就是你把事情搞定的方式。你得想清楚"AI 在这里能做什么、我在哪里加分"，而不是传统意义上"我先想自己的价值、再用 AI 增强"。在这里，心态彻底反转了。不过我不觉得 AI 在取代每个人的工作，所以请别把它当成那句陈词滥调。我常把 AI 叫做"帮我搭起平台的平均智力"，然后我在上面加上我的人脑思考和创造力，把它推到下一层。但至少我能用 AI 飞快地搞定这个基础层。所以从这个角度，如果你想在"什么叫 AI 原生的员工、怎么用这些 AI 工具"上实现跨越，你应该去 AI 公司。但如果你知道你的超能力在于更结构化、更明确、在某件事上高度专精——因为在 AI 公司，它们都相当小，所以你得很会泛化、在很多你平时可能不拥有的领域有ownership——那你就不该加入，因为 AI 公司迟早也会变得更稳定。所以只是时间问题，看你什么时候加入合适。我就想敦促大家去看清自己的超能力和真正打动自己的那种环境，这样你才能开心，因为对错误性格的人来说，这很快就会导致 burnout。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. My sense is if you want work-life balance, don't join one of these companies, because that's just not the way they work.
turns.zh: 对。我的感觉是，如果你想要工作生活平衡，就别加入这类公司，因为它们就不是那样运作的。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: I don't know if I'd go that far. I mean, I have family, I have two kids. I feel like I have a very good work-life balance, but I put in boundaries for myself. I know when I need time off because I know when my brain starts to overheat, so to speak. But I also know that work is my hobby and it's my passion, and this is the best work of my life that I'm doing right now. There's no other place that I'd rather be than to be here. (01:12:33): So I think that you just need to be more careful about setting your own boundaries that you know you need. But I mean, let's face it, I don't think anybody has work-life balance, regardless of a company that they work at, even at Google or Microsoft or any of the others. I think everybody's freaking out and running as fast as they can, it's just they're running it in different structures.
turns.zh: 我不知道我会不会说得那么绝对。我是说，我有家庭，有两个孩子。我觉得我的工作生活平衡很好，但我给自己划了边界。我知道什么时候需要休息，因为我清楚我的大脑什么时候开始"过热"了。但我也知道，工作就是我的爱好、我的热情，这是我这辈子做过的最好的工作。没有别的地方我更想待，就是这里。所以我觉得你只要更小心地守好自己的边界、你知道自己需要的边界。但说实话，我不觉得谁真有工作生活平衡，不管在哪家公司，哪怕 Google、Microsoft 还是别的。我觉得大家都在吓疯了地全速狂奔，只是跑在不同的结构里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm really glad you said that and corrected me there, that it is possible to work at a company, one of, if not the fastest-growing company in history and actually have work-life balance to get sleep, to spend time with your kids and family.
turns.zh: 我很高兴你纠正了我，说真的，在一家——如果不是史上增长最快、也是其中之一——的公司工作，还能有工作生活平衡、能睡好、能陪孩子和家人，这是可能的。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: You just have to protect it ruthlessly, but you also need to be realistic with how much is expected out of you, and you need to feel confident that you'll be able to deliver it. And by the way, you won't be able to deliver it unless you use AI in many aspects of your work life. So that's the piece that helps you actually get to hit those expectations of outcomes that you need to do and the velocity. But I'm very protective of my personal time with kids. Why did I have children if I'm not going to spend time with them? So those are part of the non-negotiables that I bring along with me in every single work.
turns.zh: 你只要 ruthlessly 地保护它，但你也要对"被期望做到什么程度"现实一点，并且要对自己能交付有信心。顺便说，你做不到交付，除非你在工作生活的很多方面都用 AI。所以正是这一点帮你真正达到那些你必须做到的结果预期和速度。但我非常保护我跟孩子相处的私人时间。我为什么要生孩子，如果我不花时间陪他们？所以这些是我带进每一份工作的不可妥协项。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For people that maybe have trouble setting boundaries or just not good at this, anything, what works for you? Is it as easy as just telling people, "Here's where I need to leave"? What advice do you have for people to set boundaries like that?
turns.zh: 对那些可能不擅长划边界、或者就不太会的人，有什么管用的？你是怎么做的？是不是就跟人说"我得几点走"这么简单？你对大家设边界有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: So first of all, I would not think about it as a work-life balance. There's no such thing as balance. So balance feels like, "Oh, I have enough time for everything." (01:14:05): I don't have enough time for anything, but I prioritize my family in some moments, I prioritize work in other moments, and I don't try to balance the two. I go where I'm needed and where I go, and I feel like I'm not going to regret the choices that I'm making today. So I'm constantly trying to put myself in the future and say, "Will I resent myself if I make this choice right now?" And if the answer is yes, I don't make that choice. (01:14:29): And sometimes I have to say no to Anton and say, "I can't make it," or, "I won't be there. I need to be here with my family," or, "Today I need to cancel my day. My kid is sick and he needs me, and I need to take him to the doctor." (01:14:43): So I think that just making in the moment, in every day, when sometimes in-the-hour decisions, to me, works better than trying to balance something that is completely unachievable and it feels overwhelming to even think about. But I prioritize this in my sleep, my health, my workout schedule, my kids, my family, my husband, and just my downtime because I know that I'm most creative once I have separation from work, because then I come in with all cylinders firing and I have so many more ideas about it. So to me, it's actually part of doing my best work is to take time off.
turns.zh: 首先，我不会把它想成"工作生活平衡"。根本没有平衡这回事。平衡给我的感觉是"哦，我什么都有足够时间"。我什么都没有足够时间，但我有些时刻优先家庭，有些时刻优先工作，我不去试图平衡两者。我去我需要去的地方，我不去后悔我今天做的选择。所以我不断把自己放到未来去想"如果我现在做这个选择，将来会怨恨自己吗？"如果是，我就不做那个选择。有时候我得跟 Anton 说"我去不了"或者"我不在，我得陪家人"，或者"今天我要取消日程，孩子病了需要我，我得带他看医生"。所以我觉得，与其试图平衡一件根本做不到、想起来就让人崩溃的事，不如在每一个当下、甚至每小时去做决定，对我来说更管用。但我优先的是：我的睡眠、健康、健身计划、孩子、家庭、丈夫，还有我的休息时间，因为我知道一旦我跟工作拉开距离，我最有创造力，回来时全身火力全开，会有多得多的想法。所以对我而言，把时间抽出来，本身就是把工作做到最好的部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really great advice. I want to touch on what it's like to work at Lovable because it feels like Lovable is at the cutting edge of what working in product is going to be. So you mentioned a little bit about how you're always talking to AI, asking questions. Is there any other kind of anecdotes of just how people operate at Lovable that is really unique or weird or funny or interesting that might be helpful for people to try in their company?
turns.zh: 这建议真的很好。我想聊聊在 Lovable 工作是什么样，因为感觉 Lovable 处在"未来产品工作会长什么样"的最前沿。你提到你们一直在跟 AI 对话、问问题。还有什么别的轶事，关于 Lovable 的人怎么运作，是特别、奇怪、好笑或有趣的，可能对别的公司也有启发？

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, we use Lovable at Lovable a lot. All of our internal tools are built on Lovables. We actually have our first hackathon on Lovable happening next week, where our entire company is just going to take full day to vibe code and see what we actually have happen. We prototype everything on Lovable. So our specs, yeah, we do still have a written spec, but it always accompanied by a lovable prototype that everybody can interact with and to click around with and provide feedback. And everybody bunches in and also does some edits if they have any better ideas. (01:16:16): So I create mocks on Lovable. So for example, we need to make some pricing changes, or pricing page changes. I take a screenshot of our pricing page. I go to Lovable as I recreate this pricing page, make these changes, and then I send that to my engineering team saying, "Hey, this is what I want to happen." And then they take it from there. (01:16:37): And ChatGPT, I use a lot for brainstorming, especially the deep thinking mode. I love it. It takes a long time, but it's so worth it. Sometimes it has crazy ideas. Sometimes it was like, "Yeah, this is nothing new to me." So it's not interesting, but it gets me thinking and it gives me a look at the different angles. (01:16:56): And I use Granola a lot, for example, because to me, it's super helpful to get AI summaries of the meetings and it's very powerful for me. I use Wispr Flow a lot because I feel like I have no time to type anymore. So I just talk to my phone and talk to my laptop all the time in order to do it. But we're even thinking about all of the customer support automations that are done through AI. Every single aspect of what we do, question is asked, what can AI do here first, and then how we can add ourselves into the equation. (01:17:33): But Lovable for us, having unlimited credits at Lovable is a pretty awesome perk, I have to say. I sometimes have to pinch myself. I'm like, "I get paid to vibe code." It looks so fun.
turns.zh: 对。我的意思是，我们自己大量用 Lovable。我们所有内部工具都建在 Lovable 上。我们下一周就要办第一次 Lovable 内部黑客松，整个公司会拿出一整天来 vibe code，看看能搞出什么。我们什么都先在 Lovable 上做原型。我们的 specs，对，我们还是有书面 spec，但它永远配着一个 Lovable 原型，大家能交互、点来点去、给反馈。所有人都涌进来，要是有更好的点子也自己改两下。所以我会在 Lovable 上做 mock。比如我们要改定价或定价页，我截一张定价页的图，去 Lovable 把它重建出来、做那些改动，然后发给工程团队说"嘿，我要的是这个"，他们接着做。ChatGPT 我也大量用来头脑风暴，尤其是深度思考模式，我爱死它了。它慢，但太值了。有时候它想法很疯，有时候"嗯，这我早知道了"，没意思，但它让我思考，给我看不同角度。我还大量用 Granola，因为它帮我把会议做成 AI 摘要，对我超有用。我大量用 Wispr Flow，因为我觉得我都没时间打字了，所以整天对着手机和笔记本说话。我们甚至在想所有客服自动化都用 AI 做。我们做的每件事，都会先问"这里 AI 能先做什么"，然后我们怎么把自己加进这个等式。不过对我们来说，在 Lovable 有无限额度真是个很爽的福利，我有时候得掐自己一下，会想"我居然拿钱来 vibe code"，看起来太好玩了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Feel like that engineer, that vibe code engineer, he's actually getting paid to vibe code.
turns.zh: 感觉那个 vibe code 工程师，他其实是在拿钱 vibe code。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: He has my dream job. I want his job.
turns.zh: 他有我梦想的工作。我想要他的工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. Exactly.
turns.zh: 对，没错，没错。

turns.zh: 对，我入错行了。

turns.en: Oh, man. Okay. Is there anything else about Lovable? Because what I think about, actually, I interviewed the Perplexity founders back in the day years ago. (01:18:11): And now that's how everyone works. And so I'm curious, I don't know how Anton works. Is there anyone else that's just way in the future of here's how things might be?
turns.zh: 哦天。好。关于 Lovable 还有别的吗？因为我想到，其实我多年前采访过 Perplexity 的创始人。在我们去问任何人要建议之前，我们先用 ChatGPT 问了一遍，我当时就"这是我听过最离谱的事，你们怎么可能那样工作？"而现在那就是每个人的工作方式。所以我好奇，我不知道 Anton 怎么工作。还有没有别人，是已经活在未来、提前展示了"事情可能怎么运作"的？

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: So for me, especially for product and growth, and even marketing in some capacity, when I have an idea in my head, it sounds so freaking cool. And sometimes I put it on paper and it's like, "Ah, we need to do it." (01:18:34): And then I go and try to vibe code it, and I'm like, "Oh, I don't see the magic anymore," or I can't envision it anymore. (01:18:43): Or sometimes I'm like, "Yeah. Yeah," and there's more, there's more. So to me, it actually has helped really complete the ideation process for me quite a bit, because then I actually try to go and build it, and it breaks down some of the elements of what's important, what's not. So it's taking me on a product development lifecycle so much further down. And then it creates a much better communication vehicle with my engineers too, because I then can tell them exactly what's important and whatnot. (01:19:12): So to me, it's been great because sometimes we envision things that are so much better than the reality. And before, until it hands it off to design, designers would do it for us and try to make it awesome versus I often stop my ideas in tracks super early on without pushing it forward. Versus other times I might've pushed it for too far too long, even through design queue or even pitching to leadership. And I find that very powerful because it calibrates me really quickly.
turns.zh: 对我来说，尤其是产品和增长，甚至某种程度营销，当脑子里有个想法，听起来超酷。有时候我把它写下来，就"啊，我们得做"。然后我去试着 vibe code，就会"哦，我看不到那个魔法了"，或者我没法再想象它了。有时候我又"对，对"，还有、还有。所以对我而言，它其实帮我相当完整地走完了构思过程，因为我会真的去试着构建，它就把哪些重要、哪些不重要拆开来。它把我的产品开发周期往前推了好多。然后它也让跟工程师的沟通好得多，因为我可以精确告诉他们什么重要、什么不重要。所以对我来说它很棒，因为有时候我们构想的东西比现实好太多。以前，在交给设计之前，设计师会帮我们做、想办法做得惊艳，而我常常在很早的阶段就把想法掐断、不往前推。另一些时候我又可能推得太久太远，哪怕排进了设计队列、甚至 pitched 给领导。我发现这很有力量，因为它极快地校准了我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. Last question. I want to talk about something that you've written about that I think it's a really important topic, something that we should surface, is you wrote this post called I'm Worried About Women In Tech. Talk about what you're seeing here, what you're noticing, what you think might be going in the wrong direction.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好，最后一个问题。我想聊一个你写过、我觉得很重要的话题，我们应该把它摆上台面——你写了篇帖子叫《我担心科技界的女性》。讲讲你在这里看到了什么、注意到了什么，觉得什么可能在往错误的方向走。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yeah. There's actually conflicting data points about how women... You're talking about women, right?
turns.zh: 对。其实关于女性……你说的是女性，对吧？有一些互相矛盾的数据点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, women in tech.
turns.zh: 对，科技界的女性。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Women in tech? Yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 科技界的女性？对，对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: There's conflicting data points about how women are keeping up with AI technology and wave, because there's a bunch of reports that has been done that show massive gap between women adopting AI versus men adopting AI, which points the story that men are just widening the gap of accessibility for technology. And whoever's adopting AI right now is getting paid the most, gets the most opportunities. I mean, we're seeing insane acqui-hires right now, where people are getting paid more for their talent than for the companies that they've created. And that's a really interesting trend that is occurring, and a lot of it is fueled on this wave of AI. (01:20:47): And women are not really present there. If you can think about one million-dollar acqui-hire that has been in the news that is a woman, I can't think of one. If you look at AI companies and their CEOs, most of it is men. If you look at the company's composition in AI companies, it's mostly men. To me, this really came to the head of when I came to Lovable, and I'm like, "It's pink, it's purple brand. It's a heart. It's lovable." I'm like, "I'm sure this is where it's 50/50 men versus a woman." (01:21:20): And although we don't collect this information, but just through third-party autofill, we saw it's like 20% at most. And I'm like, "What is happening? Not again. Why is this, again, not being adopted by a woman?" (01:21:35): And obviously I don't know all of the answers. I think that this is early on that we can shortcut it. And by the way, I also don't want to put this as a indication that men are to blame because I think men are doing wonderful job really spearheading the horizons and showing us what's possible and leading the charge. I'm just afraid that so many women are stuck in that latent majority that is just not catching up. And my worry is that it's going to affect the hireable talent. It's going to step us back again in the composition of the workplace, of the diversity. And maybe it matters, maybe it doesn't, like whichever side that you sit on. But I think that it needs to be built for everybody in the world, and for that, it needs to be built by a representative sample of people that are behind the product as well. (01:22:23): So I just find it fascinating that even when the barrier to building has been lowered versus you don't need computer science degree, which I appreciate there's not that many women that are getting. We're still seeing the gaping gap on the adoption between genders, which, I don't know, there's something very frustrating about that.
turns.zh: 关于女性怎么跟上 AI 技术和这波浪潮，有一些互相矛盾的数据点，因为有好几份报告显示，女性采用 AI 和男性采用 AI 之间存在巨大差距，指向"男性正在把技术的可及性差距拉得更大"这个故事。而现在谁在采用 AI，谁就拿钱最多、机会最多。我的意思是，我们现在看到疯狂的 acqui-hire（人才收购），人们为自己的才华拿到的钱，比他们创立的公司还多。这是一个正在发生的很有意思的趋势，而且很大程度是这波 AI 浪潮在推。而女性在那里基本缺席。你能想到一个上了新闻的、价值百万美元的 acqui-hire 是女性的吗？我想不出一个。你看 AI 公司及其 CEO，大多是男性。你看 AI 公司的人员构成，也大多是男性。这个在我来 Lovable 时彻底摆到了台面上——我心想"这是粉色、紫色品牌，一颗心，叫 Lovable（可爱）"，我"我打赌这里肯定是男女 50/50"。虽然我们不收集这个信息，但通过第三方自动填充，我们看到最多也就 20%。我就"发生了什么？又来了？为什么女性又没跟上？"我显然不知道所有答案。我觉得现在还早，我们可以走捷径绕过去。顺便说，我也不想把这说成是在怪男性，因为我觉得男性在开拓疆界、向我们展示什么是可能的、带头冲锋上，做得非常棒。我只是害怕太多女性卡在那个"潜在多数"里，就是追不上来。我担心这会影响可雇佣的人才，会让职场的构成、多元化又倒退一步。也许这重要、也许不重要，看你站在哪边。但我觉得这东西得为全世界的每个人而建，而要做到这点，它也得由具有代表性的人群来搭建，也就是做产品背后的人。所以我只是觉得，哪怕现在构建的门槛已经降低了——你不需要计算机科学学位，我很欣慰女性拿这个学位的不多——我们仍然看到性别之间 adoption 上的巨大鸿沟，这让我有种说不清的沮丧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. The thing that struck with me from your post is there has been a lot of progress being made in the last decade, and now AI is just kind of turning it all back, turning it all around.
turns.zh: 对。我从你帖子里最受触动的是，过去十年我们取得了很大进步，而现在 AI 正把它全部扭转、全部反过来。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Hopefully not. I think that we're early on enough that we can bridge the gap. I think sometimes women just need space and ability to discover it, and that's what we're doing at Lovable. We have this initiative, SheBuilds, where we create a hackathon for women only and we give them unlimited access to Lovable for 48 hours, and they come together as a community and they build together. And there's beautiful things that start to come out of it, which I've never anticipated before. But so many women in that hackathon for us build help with their elderly parents or with their kids or with the household or for their church group or for the kids' basketball team solutions, which have hyper-local, hyper-relevant, very needed for what they need in their life and something that was never been able to build before because of how expensive software was, because it would never going to become potentially a hundred-million-dollar companies, but it also doesn't need to be anymore. (01:24:01): So I just want to bring women to build more and vibe code more so we can have more diversity in software that is even created because I think that we all have a unique take on what problems that we can solve, and I want everybody's voices to be heard.
turns.zh: 希望不是。我觉得现在还够早，我们可以弥合这个差距。我觉得有时候女性只是需要空间和去发现它的能力，而这正是我们在 Lovable 做的事。我们有个叫 SheBuilds 的活动，专门为女性办黑客松，给她们 48 小时无限使用 Lovable，她们作为一个社区聚在一起、一起构建。会冒出一些我从没预料到的美好的东西。我们那个黑客松里很多女性，构建的是帮年迈父母、帮孩子、帮家务、帮教会小组、帮孩子篮球队的解决方案——这些都是高度本地化、高度相关、她们生活里非常需要，而以前因为软件太贵根本做不出来的东西；因为它永远不会成为潜在的亿万公司，但现在也不需要成为那样了。所以我就想把更多女性带进来、构建更多、vibe code 更多，这样哪怕在"被创造出来的软件"里也能有更多元化，因为我觉得我们每个人对能解决什么问题，都有独特的视角，我想让每个人的声音都被听到。

turns.en: I'll give the URL for SheBuilds. I pulled it up while you're talking, shebuilds.lovable.app.
turns.zh: 我把 SheBuilds 的网址给你们。你说话时我搜了一下，shebuilds.lovable.app。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. I think there's lots of glimmers of hope. I think we can just all lean in and make sure that nobody's left behind in this wave. And that's not to stop people that are marching ahead. This is just to open up opportunities for everybody around us.
turns.zh: 对，绝对。我觉得有很多丝希望。我觉得我们都能往里使把劲，确保这波浪潮里没人被落下。这不是要让往前冲的人停下，只是给身边的每个人打开机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And we'll link to that post if people want to get a deeper perspective, what you're saying. Elena, is there anything else that you wanted to share? Is there anything else you want to remind people of before we get to your one-question lightning round?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好，所以还是有点希望的微光。我们会在节目里链到那篇帖子，如果大家想更深入地了解你的观点。Elena，还有什么想分享的吗？在进入你的一问闪电轮之前，还有什么想提醒大家的？

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: I guess the only other thing that I will share is for AI companies when it comes to hiring. It's really interesting, also, kind of the shift in the type of personas that end up being hired that I see. For me, at least it's quite different compared to anywhere that I worked before. And that is, there's this narrative going in the market always that new hires, sorry, new grads have no jobs in the market left because all of the entry-level jobs are automated. (01:26:07): I actually think that's quite false, because new grads, especially AI-native new grads... So it's very important for kids that are entering into the, I shouldn't say kids, young adults that are entering into the workforce that they really know AI, which there's another really big issue that our schools are not teaching AI students. So this is something else that we need to fix as a category, because otherwise we're literally setting up our young for a complete failure. But I think it's incredible to see some of those new graduates come in and what they're capable of doing. (01:26:43): We have multiple new graduates at Lovable that are working, and I learned so much from them. And you need to obviously have the right atmosphere where people with experience, like a old guard like me, that can look at the new guard and really hear them and see them and really change the way that I operate based on how they do things. So make sure that you bring some of that fresh talent that doesn't understand any of the baggage that we came from and that can really look at the future in technology and what can unlock from a completely new lens. So highly recommend putting those into your team as little fireballs that are going to be sometimes hard to contain but can start the best initiatives for you forward. (01:27:32): And then it's also interesting that there's a really high demand for ex-founders now, for those people that truly have a lot of agency and high autonomy. So instead of just having people that have been working in the corporate world, the failed startup founders are now hot demand for a lot of these AI companies. So these personas that we traditionally would not prioritize in companies to hire are now becoming the hottest commodity and the highest-going talent, which I think is fascinating and is the wonderful thing that is changing how the culture inside operates.
turns.zh: 我想分享的另一件事，是关于 AI 公司招聘时，我看到的被招进来的人物类型，也很有意思，某种程度上是一种转变。对我来说，这跟我以前待过的任何地方都相当不同。市面上有一种说法，说因为所有初级岗位都被自动化了，新毕业生在市场上没工作剩下了。我其实觉得这相当假，因为新毕业生，尤其是 AI 原生的新毕业生……所以对进入职场的年轻人——我不该说孩子，是年轻成年人——来说，真正懂 AI 非常重要，而这里有个更大的问题：我们的学校没在教学生 AI。这是作为这个品类我们需要解决的另一个问题，否则我们简直是在让年轻人走向彻底的失败。但我看到一些新毕业生进来、以及他们的能力，觉得不可思议。Lovable 有好几个新毕业生在工作，我从他们身上学到超多。你显然得有对的氛围，让有经验的人——像我这种老 guard——能看着新 guard、真正听进去、看见他们，并根据他们做事的方式改变我自己的运作。所以务必把一些没有我们这些包袱、能用全新视角看技术未来和能解锁什么的新鲜人才带进团队。我强烈建议把他们放进你的团队，当作那些有时候难管、但能为你启动最好倡议的小火球。还有一点很有意思，现在对前创始人的需求非常高，对那些真正有很强能动性和高自主权的人。所以不再只是要有在公司体系里工作过的人，那些失败过的创业创始人，现在成了很多 AI 公司的抢手货。这些我们传统上不会优先招的人物类型，现在成了最热门的商品、薪酬最高的人才，我觉得这很迷人，也是改变公司内部文化运作的一件美事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really interesting and really empowering, just this idea that if you need grad, there's hope. You're not going to be out of a job.
turns.zh: 这真的很有意思，也很赋能——就是"如果你是新毕业生，还有希望，你不会失业"这个想法。

turns.speaker: Elena Verna
turns.en: Absolutely. Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对。绝对。
